findings.title: Token-response and OIDC-discovery error messages are not harmonized (rust lowercase, kotlin/php/swift/elixir/go variants; python/ruby accept non-string endpoints)
findings.description: R8-7 harmonized many messages but not these. Canonical (java/csharp/python/ruby/node/dart): invalid JSON → 'Token response is not valid JSON: <detail>', non-object → 'Token response is not a JSON object', missing → 'Token response missing or empty access_token field'. Divergent: rust 'failed to parse token response: …' and lowercase 'token response missing or empty access_token field', and no non-object check (a JSON array yields the missing-token message); kotlin 'Token response is not a JSON object: <detail>' for invalid JSON; php no 'not valid JSON' message, and a JSON list passes is_array so `[]` reports missing access_token; swift and elixir 'Token response is not a valid token JSON object' for both cases; go reports a JSON array as 'Token response is not valid JSON: json: cannot unmarshal array…' and `null` as missing access_token. OIDC discovery: java alone has 'OIDC discovery document field is not a string: <f>'; kotlin 'not a JSON object: <detail>' for invalid JSON; php/elixir/swift report invalid JSON as 'not a JSON object' (swift also for a non-string endpoint, go as 'not valid JSON'); python (`if not authorization_endpoint`) and ruby (`.to_s.strip.empty?`) accept a non-string truthy endpoint (e.g. 123) and build a delegate with it; whitespace-only endpoints are rejected by rust/go/swift/ruby/elixir but accepted by the rest.

evidence.quote: "token response missing or empty access_token field"
"Token response is not a JSON object: ${e.message}"
if (!is_array($responseBody)) { throw new OAuth2TokenException('Token response is not a JSON object');

findings.title: Unclamped expires_in / discovery max-age arithmetic: swift traps, rust panics, java/csharp/ruby throw raw runtime exceptions, kotlin/go silently wrap
findings.description: A server-supplied huge/infinite lifetime is not clamped before date arithmetic. swift: Int(d.rounded(.down)) traps the process for expires_in > Int.max (e.g. 1e20, verified with a probe: 'Double value cannot be converted to Int'). rust: f64→u64 saturates, then Instant::now() + Duration::from_secs(u64::MAX-30) panics ('overflow when adding duration to instant'); same for OIDC max-age. java: textual branch of parseExpiresIn has no NaN/Infinity guard, so "Infinity"/"1e400"/1e20 become Long.MAX_VALUE and Instant.plusSeconds throws ArithmeticException: long overflow (probed); values > ~3.1e16 throw DateTimeException; OIDC max-age likewise. csharp: DateTimeOffset.AddSeconds throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException for ~2.5e11..9.2e18. ruby: Float("1e400").floor raises FloatDomainError (not rescued; probed). kotlin: (expiresIn-30)*1000 overflows → expiry in the past → refetch on every call; go: time.Duration(n)*time.Second overflows for > ~9.2e9 s. dart: Duration/DateTime.add range (unverified). python/node/php/elixir cache normally. These escape as non-SDK exceptions (or a crash) instead of the OAuth2TokenError/'stale' contract every other edge case follows. Fix: clamp expires_in and max-age to a sane ceiling (e.g. 1 year) in all 12 and add a unit row for 1e20 and "Infinity".
findings.note: done in rust; still open for csharp, dart, go, java, kotlin, ruby, swift

rust.note: Rust side only. expires_in and Cache-Control max-age are clamped to 31,536,000 s (one year) before the Instant arithmetic, which used to panic for huge values.

findings.title: csharp normalizes redirect_uri through System.Uri.ToString() (trailing slash, default port, host case, unescaping) — bytes differ from the configured value
findings.description: csharp types redirectUri as System.Uri and emits `_redirectUri.ToString()` in both the authorize URL and the code-exchange body. Uri.ToString() returns the canonical unescaped form: a host-only redirect 'http://localhost:8080' becomes 'http://localhost:8080/', ':443' is dropped, the host is lower-cased, and percent-escapes are unescaped before EscapeDataString re-escapes them. OPs compare redirect_uri by exact string (RFC 6749 §3.1.2.3), so csharp can fail with redirect_uri_mismatch where the other 11 send the string verbatim. R8-F2 only covers the OIDC endpoint being a Uri. Use OriginalString (or keep redirect_uri a string). PLAUSIBLE: .NET behaviour stated from documentation, not executed here.

csharp.note: Both redirect_uri sites (authorize URL and code-exchange body) now use Uri.OriginalString instead of ToString(), so no trailing slash, default-port drop or host lowercasing.
csharp.test: OAuth2AuthCodeAuthenticatorTest.mustache: AuthorizationUrlSendsRedirectUriVerbatim and CodeExchangeSendsRedirectUriVerbatim (host-only URI, and :443 with mixed-case host)

findings.title: elixir auth-code/OIDC: exchange_code returns a new struct the Client never sees, so API calls keep raising 'Must call exchange_code'
findings.description: In the other 11, exchangeCode on the authenticator instance the client holds completes the flow. In elixir, OAuth2AuthorizationCodeAuthenticator.exchange_code returns `%{self | token_exchanged: true}` — the flag lives in the struct, not in the shared token-manager Agent — and Client.new stores its own copy, so every API call through the Client raises 'Must call exchange_code before making API requests'. For OIDC, set_api_client returns `%{self | api_client: client}` only on the Client's copy, so calling exchange_code/build_authorization_url on the user's struct hits the `api_client: nil` clause and raises 'ApiClient has not been injected'. The elixir tests only exercise these by calling set_api_client manually and auth_headers directly, never through Client.new. Not forced: the SDK already shares mutable state via Agents (token manager, discovery_cache); the exchanged flag/api_client should live there too.

evidence.quote: def auth_headers(%__MODULE__{token_exchanged: false}) do raise "Must call exchange_code before making API requests"

elixir.note: The token_exchanged flag now lives in the shared OAuth2TokenManager agent (mark_exchanged/1 and exchanged?/1), so any copy of the auth-code authenticator is ready after exchange_code. OIDC set_api_client also stores the ApiClient in the shared discovery_cache agent, and resolve_delegate adopts it when a copy has api_client nil. Dialyzer needed a no_return spec on the new raise helper.
elixir.test: test/oauth2_auth_code_authenticator_test.mustache: 'exchange_code readies the authenticator without using its return value'; test/openid_connect_authenticator_test.mustache: "exchange_code on the caller's copy readies the client's copy"

findings.title: exchangeCode() is silently ignored when a token is cached or a refresh token exists (goes through the caching getAccessToken)
findings.description: Uniform defect. exchangeCode/exchange_code calls tokenManager.getAccessToken(tokenUrl, codeParams), which first returns any still-valid cached token, and otherwise tries the refresh_token grant (and returns its result on success) before ever POSTing grant_type=authorization_code. A second exchangeCode (user re-login / account switch / scope upgrade on a long-lived authenticator, or OIDC) therefore never sends the new code: the old identity's token keeps being used and tokenExchanged is set to true. The code exchange should bypass the cache and refresh path (direct fetch, replacing access/refresh tokens).

findings.title: java auth-code getAuthHeaders NPEs when the OP issued no refresh_token and the access token expired
findings.description: java puts tokenManager.getRefreshToken() (null when the OP returned no refresh_token) straight into the params map; once the access token expires, fetchToken form-encodes the null value and URLEncoder.encode(null) throws NullPointerException out of getAuthHeaders. kotlin/csharp/php/python/ruby/node/dart/go/rust/swift/elixir substitute "" and POST refresh_token= which surfaces as the typed OAuth2ServerError (400). Fix: `?: ""` parity (or better, all 12 raise a typed 'token expired and no refresh token' error instead of sending an empty refresh grant).

java.note: OAuth2AuthorizationCodeAuthenticator.getAuthHeaders now puts '' when getRefreshToken() is null. The OP's 400 surfaces as a typed OAuth2ServerException instead of a NullPointerException from URLEncoder.

findings.title: A zero or negative timeout means something different in each SDK; only rust validates it
findings.description: Every builder takes the timeout with no range check except rust, whose build() returns ConfigurationError::InvalidTimeout for a negative value. The other 11 pass the raw number to their HTTP library, giving library-specific results (from library semantics, not run here). java: Duration.ofMillis(<=0) passed to HttpClient.Builder.connectTimeout and HttpRequest timeout throws a raw IllegalArgumentException at client construction or request time. kotlin: Ktor HttpTimeout requires values > 0, raw IAE. csharp: HttpClient.Timeout throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException for 0, but -1 equals Timeout.InfiniteTimeSpan, so timeout(-1) silently means no timeout. python: urllib3.Timeout(total<=0) raises ValueError on every request rather than at configuration. node: AbortSignal.timeout(-1) throws RangeError per request (verified locally), and 0 aborts immediately, giving NetworkTimeoutError. go: http.Client sets a deadline only when Timeout > 0, so 0 and negative both mean no timeout. rust: 0 is a zero deadline (immediate timeout), negative is rejected at build. php: max_duration=0 is Symfony's 'unlimited'. dart: Future.timeout with a negative duration fires immediately. Same input, different accept/reject and wire outcome. Under the error contract a negative timeout is a caller mistake and should be rejected at configuration, as rust does. A shared rule (reject < 0, decide whether 0 means no deadline) is needed.

evidence.quote: public Builder timeout(@Nullable Integer timeout) { this.timeout = timeout; return this; }
timeout: non_neg_integer() | nil (typespec only, not enforced)

findings.title: Per-operation server codegen emits duplicate types when two servers of one operation share a variable or a description
findings.description: AbstractBetterCodegen.enrichOperationServers builds serverVariables per variant and never de-duplicates. Every api template emits the variable's enum inside the `{{#variants}}` loop. An operation with two servers that both declare an enum variable `region` is a normal pattern, for example `https://{region}.a.com` and `https://{region}.b.com`. It produces two declarations of the same enum type: compile errors in java (nested enum), kotlin, csharp (CS0101), go, dart, rust and swift; a TS duplicate identifier in node; silent last-wins redefinition in python and php (separate file overwritten), which is wrong if the enum sets differ; and a redefining-module warning in elixir and ruby, which elixir's --warnings-as-errors turns fatal. Variant names come from PascalCase(description) or `Server<index>`, so two servers with the same description, or one starting with a digit, also collide or produce invalid identifiers. The petstore only has getMultiServerPetInfo, where just one of the two servers has a variable, so this is untested.

findings.title: Test gaps: no test covers CA sole-anchor, garbage-CA rejection outside 3 SDKs, proxy failure classes, timeout <= 0, or a shared per-operation server variable
findings.description: These gaps let several findings above go unnoticed. (1) An unparseable CA file is tested only in java (garbagePemCaCertPathThrowsIllegalArgumentException), kotlin (ClientTest) and dart. The other 9 test only a missing file, so rust's lazy from_pem passes. Add a garbage-PEM row to every DefaultApiClient unit test. (2) Nothing checks that caCertPath is the sole trust anchor, so the dart/rust/ruby add-to-system-roots split goes unseen. Petstore/fixture expansion: point a client with caCertPath=fixtures/certs/ca.pem at a TLS endpoint signed by a different CA (a second chasm cert, or the publicly trusted proxy path) and expect NetworkError. (3) Proxy validation tests use one garbage string, except go (ftp, 'http://', socks5) and node (ftp). Missing-host, non-http scheme, upper-case scheme and empty-string cases are untested in 10 SDKs, and no SDK asserts the message. Add it.each/table rows to each TransportOptionsTest. (4) Negative/zero timeout is tested only in rust (test_transport_options_negative_timeout_is_rejected). (5) Server-variable message: no full-message assertion anywhere. (6) Petstore spec expansion: add an operation with two servers that share an enum variable (for example `https://{region}.a.example.com` and `https://{region}.b.example.com`), one with an undescribed server (a second `Server0` across operations, for csharp), and a URL template that repeats a variable. That catches the duplicate-type codegen defect, the csharp namespace collisions and node's first-occurrence replace. (7) swift: all HTTPS/CA/proxy integration tests sit under `#if !os(Linux)` and CI runs Linux, so the PEM-vs-DER, Linux-silent-TLS and HTTPSProxy-key bugs have zero coverage. A Linux-runnable unit test should at least assert that verifySsl(false) and caCertPath throw like proxyUnsupported.

findings.title: csharp declares per-operation server types un-prefixed at namespace level (cross-operation collisions) and emits a duplicate <summary>
findings.description: The other 11 scope per-operation server types: java/kotlin nest them in the sealed interface; python/go/node/ruby/php/dart/rust/swift prefix them with the operation (GetMultiServerPetInfoServerRegional, GetStagingPetInfoServerEnvironment); elixir nests modules. csharp emits `Server0`, `Primary`, `Regional`, `StagingServer`, `RegionValue`, `EnvironmentValue` and `VersionValue` as top-level types in PetstoreClient.Api. Two operations that each have an undescribed server both produce `public sealed class Server0`, which fails with CS0101. The same happens for two operations with an `environment` enum variable or servers with the same description, and a model of the same name causes CS0104 ambiguity through `using PetstoreClient.Models;`. Separately, for an undescribed server without variables the template prints the summary twice (lines 48-50 and again at 74-76), so the golden has two identical `<summary>` lines on Server0.

findings.title: dart's only tracing opt-in (TraceContextUtil.propagator) is not exported from the public library
findings.description: dart cannot detect OpenTelemetry at runtime, so tracing works only if the application sets `TraceContextUtil.propagator = ...`, as the class doc says. The package barrel lib/petstore_client.dart exports configuration, server_configuration, servers and transport_options but not src/trace_context_util.dart. Users must import `package:petstore_client/src/trace_context_util.dart`, an implementation import that the implementation_imports lint flags, and the SDK's own test does exactly that. go (SetTraceContextPropagator) and swift (public enum TraceContextUtil.propagator) expose their registration hook publicly. node and rust keep their helper internal, but they need no registration (runtime detection and a cargo feature).

evidence.quote: static void Function(Map<String, String> headers)? propagator;

dart.note: Added export 'src/trace_context_util.dart' to the barrel. The trace test now imports the public library, so it will not compile without the export.
dart.test: trace_context_util_test.mustache: all tests; they use TraceContextUtil via package:petstore_client/petstore_client.dart

findings.title: java, kotlin and swift trust only the first certificate in a caCertPath bundle
findings.description: java and kotlin load the CA with CertificateFactory.generateCertificate(fis), which reads one certificate, and store a single 'ca' entry. swift calls SecCertificateCreateWithData once and anchors one certificate. The other 9 trust every certificate in the file: csharp ImportFromPemFile collection, go AppendCertsFromPEM, python load_verify_locations, ruby/php/elixir ca_file/cafile/cacertfile, node `ca` buffer, dart setTrustedCertificates, and rust (reqwest add_to_rustls iterates all PEM certs). A bundle with a root and an intermediate, or two roots during a CA rotation, works in 9 SDKs and fails TLS in java/kotlin/swift whenever the server chains to any cert but the first. The fix is generateCertificates() with every entry added to the trust store.
findings.note: done in java, kotlin; still open for swift

kotlin.note: Kotlin part only. loadCaCertTrustManager (now internal) uses generateCertificates and adds every cert to the trust store as ca-N. An empty file still raises through the existing IllegalArgumentException path.
kotlin.test: DefaultApiClientTest.kt: 'trusts every certificate in a multi-certificate CA bundle' (server.pem then ca.pem; expects 2 accepted issuers)

java.note: Java part: new buildPinnedTrustStore uses generateCertificates and adds every certificate (ca-0, ca-1, ...). An empty file still fails fast as IllegalArgumentException. The kotlin and swift parts are outside this scope.

findings.title: swift (Apple): an http:// proxy only covers http destinations, so HTTPS API calls bypass it
findings.description: swift builds connectionProxyDictionary from the proxy URL's own scheme. For https://proxy it sets only HTTPSEnable/HTTPSProxy/HTTPSPort; for http://proxy it sets only HTTPEnable/HTTPProxy/HTTPPort. In CFNetwork, the HTTP* keys select the proxy for http:// requests and the HTTPS* keys select it for https:// requests. So with the usual http://proxy:3128, every https:// request goes direct, bypassing the proxy. With an https:// proxy URL, http:// requests go direct instead. Every other SDK sends all traffic through the configured proxy (java ProxySelector.of, go http.ProxyURL, node ProxyAgent, python ProxyManager, etc.). Only on Apple platforms; Linux throws proxyUnsupported, so CI never runs this path. Not runtime-verified here; based on CFNetwork key semantics.

findings.title: swift on Linux silently ignores verifySsl=false and caCertPath, while a proxy on Linux throws
findings.description: The whole URLSession server-trust challenge handler is inside `#if canImport(Security)`. On Linux (FoundationNetworking) there is no handler, so verifySsl(false) does not disable verification and caCertPath is not applied. Only the file's readability is checked, and the system trust store is used. Both settings are dropped without any error. For the comparable platform limit, swift throws ConfigurationError.proxyUnsupported when a proxy is configured on Linux. So swift is internally inconsistent, and on Linux it accepts settings that do nothing; the other 11 honour both. The platform limit is forced, but staying silent is not: it should throw like proxyUnsupported. Linux is the platform CI uses, and all swift HTTPS tests are excluded there.

evidence.quote:
#if canImport(Security)
    func urlSession(_ session: URLSession, didReceive challenge: ...

findings.suspected_forced_reason: swift-corelibs-foundation does not surface server-trust challenges; forced to be unsupported, but not forced to be silent

findings.title: A required discriminator property that is absent (DryFood/WetFood.foodType) is accepted by 8 SDKs and rejected by 4; elixir's and go's comments contradict their code
findings.description: `foodType` is `required` in DryFood/WetFood. The generator gives it a synthetic default from the discriminator mapping (applyDiscriminatorDefault, AbstractBetterCodegen.java ~5640). Decoding a DryFood with no `foodType` key is then accepted and filled with 'dry' by java (field initializer, not a creator param), kotlin (`= "dry"`), csharp (not `required`), php (assertRequiredPresent skips defaulted ctor params), python (`default="dry"`), ruby (`Types::Required.default('dry')`), node (constructor fills it) and elixir (required_fields excludes it). It is rejected by go (dry_food.go:68-71), dart (dry_food.dart:25), rust (no serde default, dry_food.rs:16) and swift (`container.decode`, DryFood.swift:38). elixir's required_fields doc says the exclusion matches 'the Go / PHP / Kotlin reference behaviour', but go rejects. go's own comment at dry_food.go:78 ('An absent field carrying a schema default is populated with that default') is dead, because the function already returned an error. Decide one rule (most likely: accept, because the default satisfies the requirement) and add a 'DryFood without foodType' decode test in all 12.

findings.title: `type: number` (weightKg): python and node are lossy on decode (python on encode too) and accept quoted strings, contradicting AGENTS' 'FIVE preserve full textual precision'
findings.description: AGENTS.md:246 lists python (`Decimal`) and node (branded `Decimal` + `JSON.rawJSON`) among the FIVE SDKs that preserve full precision. That is not true of the code. python decodes with a plain `json.loads` without `parse_float=Decimal` (object_serializer.py:220), so the value is a binary float before pydantic builds the Decimal. In pydantic 2.12, `{"weightKg": 0.1234567890123456789}` gives `Decimal('0.12345678901234568')` and 12345678901234567890.5 gives `Decimal('12345678901234567000')`. Encoding goes through `float(value)` (_types.py:87-90). node decodes with a bare `JSON.parse` (object-serializer.ts:274), so the number is already rounded before the Pet constructor applies `String(this.weightKg)` (pet.ts:161-162). Both also accept a JSON STRING for a `type: number` field. python's Decimal is lax, so `"12.345"` is accepted. node accepts ANY string (`"abc"`), because the only check is `typeof !== "string"` (pet.ts:163), and it then re-emits it quoted. java/kotlin/csharp reject a quoted number (jackson 2.19.4 with ALLOW_COERCION_OF_SCALARS=false gives MismatchedInputException; kotlin's BigDecimal(element.toString()) fails on the quotes). The python README even claims the field 'deserializes to decimal.Decimal' as the precision-safe path. Either fix decoding (python `parse_float=decimal.Decimal`; node a JSON.parse reviver using `context.source`) or move both to the lossy list in AGENTS.

findings.title: node's global Decimal-field registry turns string values in free-form objects into JSON numbers when their key matches any model's decimal field name
findings.description: ObjectSerializer.serialize's replacer (object-serializer.ts:360-372) checks the holder's constructor for `__decimalFields`. findings.title: go: every operation's primary doc comment is detached from its func (blank line), so godoc/gopls/staticcheck never see it — including the `// Deprecated:` marker on FindPetsByStatus/GetPetById, which is also not its own paragraph
findings.description: The go api template ends the data-method doc block with `{{#allParams}}{{#vendorExtensions.pluralExamples}}` on one line (two tags, so jmustache does not treat it as standalone). That emits a blank line between the `//` comment block and `func`. Go only treats a comment as a doc comment when it sits directly above the declaration with no blank line, so every data method (AddPet, GetPetByName, FindPetsByStatus, GetPetById, all StoreApi data methods) has NO doc comment. Two consequences: (1) `// Deprecated: This operation is deprecated.` on the primary FindPetsByStatus/GetPetById methods is not attached, so staticcheck SA1019 and gopls never flag callers; only the *WithHTTPInfo variants (which emit a correct `//` + `// Deprecated:` paragraph) are flagged. (2) Even attached, the marker sits mid-paragraph (line 678 directly after the summary, with no `//` separator line). Go's convention and staticcheck's parser only recognise a paragraph that STARTS with `Deprecated: `. The same mid-paragraph form appears on deprecated Options fields (`/* Status ... */` immediately followed by `// Deprecated:`), so FindPetsByStatusOptions.Status is not recognised as deprecated either. This contradicts the AGENTS T2-5 claim that go marks every public variant with a `// Deprecated:` doc paragraph. findings.title: A non-JSON success Content-Type on a model-returning operation gives 5 different outcomes
findings.description: Example: getPetById receives `200 text/plain "hello"` (or text/html from a proxy, or JSON mislabelled as text/plain). java stores the String in a T-typed slot, which is heap pollution, and the caller gets a ClassCastException when assigning it to a Pet. kotlin throws ClassCastException inside the SDK (`response.body as T` with reified T), and csharp throws InvalidCastException (`(T)(object)response.Body`). python, ruby, node, php and elixir silently return the raw string as the 'Pet'. dart (data=null), rust (base64-decodes the text, gets an empty string, from_value fails, .ok() gives None) and swift (`as? T` gives nil) raise the 'Expected a response body for getPetById but received none' ApiError. go returns a zero-valued Pet with a nil error, and go's own TestBaseApi_SkipsDeserializationForNonJSON locks that behaviour in. The tests disagree too: rust's equivalent test accepts any outcome, swift asserts data==nil, and java/kotlin/csharp/python only test a String return type. Pick one contract, for example a SerializationError naming the unexpected Content-Type, and assert it in every language's BaseApi test.
findings.suspected_forced_reason: none

findings.title: A response with no Content-Type on a byte/binary operation (getPetAvatar, downloadPetDocument, getPetAvatarThumbnail) decodes differently everywhere
findings.description: Every transport treats an absent Content-Type as text and returns the UTF-8-decoded string. The API layers then disagree. For a format:binary operation such as getPetAvatar: java base64-decodes that text and throws a raw IllegalArgumentException (see the separate java finding). kotlin, csharp and ruby return the UTF-8 bytes. dart tries base64 first and falls back to UTF-8. python, node, go, swift and elixir assume JSON and raise SerializationError. rust parses it as JSON and returns an EMPTY Vec on failure. php json_decode()s it to null, then settype(null,'string') gives "", which is returned as the bytes with no error. For a format:byte operation such as getPetAvatarThumbnail, whose body is a JSON string literal: python, ruby, node, php, go, rust, swift and elixir default to JSON and decode correctly. kotlin, csharp and dart return the UTF-8 bytes of the QUOTED literal, which are wrong bytes. java throws IllegalArgumentException. The dart result contradicts AGENTS 'dart defaults an absent/empty response Content-Type to JSON … matching swift/node' for byte returns. Root cause: binary and byte returns collapse to one native type, and the base layer is not told which format the operation declared. Fix: have the generator pass isBinary/isByteArray to the base layer and apply one rule. Add unit tests for both operations with no Content-Type.
findings.suspected_forced_reason: none

findings.title: Malformed base64 in a top-level format:byte response (getPetAvatarThumbnail): 3 raw platform exceptions, 2 silent decodes, contradicting AGENTS T1-10
findings.description: getPetAvatarThumbnail returns a JSON string literal holding base64. If that string is not valid base64, the error contract says every decode failure is a SerializationError. python, ruby, php, go, swift and elixir raise it. java and kotlin call java.util.Base64.getDecoder().decode(inner) outside any wrapper, so a raw IllegalArgumentException leaks. csharp's Convert.FromBase64String leaks a raw FormatException, and dart's base64Decode(inner) does the same. node uses `Buffer.from(json as string, 'base64')`, which silently drops non-alphabet characters: I confirmed that "!!not*base64??" decodes to 6 garbage bytes. rust does `.decode(...).unwrap_or_default()` and returns an EMPTY Vec. AGENTS.md (Resolved) says 'python and node reject malformed base64 on decode (node decodeBase64 validates …) matching ruby/php/elixir/go/rust'. The node top-level byte path never calls decodeBase64, and rust's top-level path is lenient, so the code contradicts that document. R7-T3 covers only model fields, not this operation-return path. Fix: route these decodes through each SDK's strict decoder or SerializationError wrapper, and add a malformed-thumbnail unit test in all 12.

findings.title: Petstore spec does not exercise several body/response shapes, so whole branches above are never generated or tested
findings.description: Several divergences above sit in code that petstore never reaches. Additions to petstore that would catch them: (a) a public (not x-internal) operation returning text/plain String, which would catch the rust/go empty-string bug; testTextPlain/testEmpty are x-internal and never generated. (b) An operation whose only response is `default` with a schema, plus a 4xx response with a declared error schema; no petstore operation declares an error-response schema or a default response, so the codegen path for operation-declared error bodies is uncovered. (c) Unit tests (no spec change needed) driving getPetPhoto with the application/json Photo variant, and getPetAvatar/getPetAvatarThumbnail with no Content-Type and with malformed base64. (d) A void operation whose server returns a text or JSON body, which would catch the kotlin ClassCastException. (e) placeOrder called without a body, which would catch the go/rust `null`. (f) Form values containing `& = + # ~ *` and non-ASCII characters, which would catch the kotlin injection and the ~/* split. (g) date-time, number and boolean fields on setPetPreferences, which would catch ruby's to_s. (h) An exact-order assertion on form and multipart bodies in every language. findings.title: java BaseApi treats an empty Content-Type as base64-binary while its own transport treats it as text
findings.description: Java's DefaultApiClient.isTextContentType("") returns true, with the comment 'A response with no Content-Type defaults to text handling', so the body is a UTF-8 String. BaseApi.isTextResponseContentType("") returns false, and its comment says 'Mirror the transport: an absent/empty Content-Type is treated as binary (base64-encoded by the transport)'. That is false. So getPetAvatar, downloadPetDocument and getPetPhoto with no Content-Type call Base64.getDecoder().decode() on decoded text. The result is a raw IllegalArgumentException leaking past the error contract, or garbage bytes when the text happens to be base64-shaped. kotlin, csharp, ruby, python and go mirror their transports correctly: all return true for empty. Fix: return true for empty in java's base_api.mustache, and add a unit test with a binary operation and no Content-Type.

findings.title: kotlin void operations throw when the success response carries a non-object body
findings.description: Kotlin routes void operations (deletePet, setPetAvatar, setPetAvatarThumbnail) through invokeApiForResult<Unit>, and that function decodes any non-empty body. A text/plain or octet-stream body (for example `200 OK` with body "Deleted") hits the non-JSON branch `response.body as T`. Because T is reified Unit, that is a checked cast, so a raw java.lang.ClassCastException escapes the SDK. A JSON body that is not an object (`true`, `[]`, `"ok"`) makes deserialize<Unit> throw SerializationException. The other 11 never decode a void operation's body: java, csharp, python, ruby, node, dart, go and elixir pass a null or empty returnType, rust and swift use invoke…ForEmptyResult, and php only populates data, per T3-15. Fix: skip decoding when T is Unit, as java does by passing returnType null. Add a void-op-with-text-body unit test to every language.

findings.title: rust and go return an empty string for a String-returning operation that gets a text/plain body
findings.description: Every transport keeps text/* bodies as decoded text: rust's is_text_content_type returns true for text/*. Yet rust's invoke_api_for_result non-JSON, non-binary branch assumes the body was base64-encoded and calls STANDARD.decode(body).unwrap_or_default(). Any text containing a space or other non-base64 character decodes to nothing, so the caller gets Some(""). Text that happens to be valid base64 decodes to garbage. go's per-operation response template only has branches for JSON and []byte, so a string (or model) return with a text/* Content-Type keeps its zero value and returns "" or a zero struct with a nil error. java, kotlin, csharp, python, ruby, node, php, dart, swift and elixir return the text verbatim, and java/kotlin/csharp/python have a test for it (returnsRawStringForNonJson). This is latent in the petstore goldens because testTextPlain is x-internal and never generated, so no public operation returns text/plain and the rust/go code paths are never exercised. Fix: rust should return the body as-is for text media types; go should add a string branch. Expose a public text/plain operation in petstore so all 12 compile and test this path.

findings.title: Post-headers body-read failure/timeout classification is tested unevenly; node asserts broad ApiError; dart arms no body-read deadline at all
findings.description: 'A connection reset/truncation AFTER headers is NetworkError(status 0, cause kept)' is asserted with the exact type in kotlin, csharp, python, dart and rust. java, php, ruby, swift and elixir have no such test; go tests only the body-read TIMEOUT variant. node's test asserts rejects.toBeInstanceOf(ApiError), which also passes if the client regressed to ApiError(200) (the source throws NetworkError, abstract-api-client.ts:507). The body-read TIMEOUT case (headers arrive, body stalls) is tested only in go and rust. dart io would fail it: Future.timeout wraps only the pending send() (headers), and streamedResponse.stream.toBytes() runs with no deadline, so a stalled body hangs forever despite TransportOptions.timeout. Add a truncated-body NetworkError test and a stalled-body NetworkTimeoutError test per SDK (exact type + statusCode 0), and give dart a body-read deadline.

findings.title: rust has no brotli decode test, and no SDK asserts the Accept-Encoding it advertises by default
findings.description: Eleven SDKs have a 'decompresses brotli response' integration test; rust has gzip and zstd only, although T3-6 added a 'br' arm (brotli::Decompressor) and 'br' to rust's Accept-Encoding and called it 'CI-validated' - nothing exercises it. Separately, every compression test passes Accept-Encoding EXPLICITLY in the request headers, so no SDK asserts the header it sends on its own. Those values are the documented forced differences (dart 'gzip, deflate'; csharp no zstd; swift none; rust/go 'gzip, deflate, br, zstd' with go's order changed in R8-8), and the decode path a server reaches when the SDK advertised the codec itself is untested. Add a rust br test (template default_api_client_test.mustache next to :657/:671), and a per-language unit test pinning the default Accept-Encoding value (asserted as the documented per-language set).

findings.title: swift depth-cap test uses 50-deep 'within' (peers 500-600) and its comment contradicts the source and AGENTS; Foundation's ~512 nesting limit makes swift's effective cap <1000
findings.description: Ten SDKs assert a 600-deep payload decodes and 1500-deep is rejected (rust 500/1500). swift asserts only nestedObjects(50) decodes. Its comment says swift 'relies on the platform decoder's guard rather than a 1000-deep pre-flight cap', which contradicts the swift source (ObjectSerializer.maxJsonDepth = 1000 with a jsonMaxDepth pre-flight) and AGENTS R6-6 ('all 12 use the 1000 depth cap'). Foundation's JSON parser has its own nesting limit (512 in swift-corelibs-foundation / swift-foundation), so a 513..1000-deep body that the other 11 accept is rejected by swift; the 50-deep 'within' value hides exactly that. Raise the swift 'within' case to 600 like peers (it will expose the limit) and either document a forced 512 cap or decode through a path without the 512 limit; fix the stale comment.

findings.title: Space-encoding assertions accept either `+` or `%20` in 7 SDKs, so the authorize-URL `%20` and token-body `+` contracts are not locked
findings.description: The resolved contract is `%20` in the authorize URL (php T1-1) and `+` in the x-www-form-urlencoded token body. For the authorize URL, php, ruby, node, dart and swift assert `scope=read%20write` exactly. java, kotlin and elixir accept `+` or `%20`, and csharp also accepts a raw space. python parses the URL with parse_qs, so `+` and `%20` look the same. go and rust check only `scope=read`. For the token body (`sendsScopes`), csharp, php, ruby and rust assert `scope=read+write`. java, kotlin, python and elixir accept either encoding (python also a raw space). dart, go and swift check only `scope=read` plus `write`. node compares the decoded value, which cannot tell the encodings apart. A regression to a default RFC 1738 encoder in the authorize URL, the T1-1 bug class, would pass in 7 SDKs. Fix: assert the exact encoded substring in every SDK, matching the php/ruby/node/dart/swift authorize tests and the csharp/php/ruby/rust body tests.

findings.title: Digit-leading property/param names give invalid identifiers in python/dart/php/rust and an unexported (silently dropped) field in go
findings.description: AbstractBetterCodegen.toVarName and toParamName send any name matching ^\d to escapeReservedWord, which was written to escape keywords. The base implementation prefixes `_`, giving `_1st`, which works for java/kotlin/node/swift/ruby/elixir. python, dart and php override it to append `_`, producing `1st_`, which is a syntax error in all three (php `$1st_`). rust overrides it to prefix `r#`, producing `r#1st`, which is not a legal raw identifier. go turns off reserved escaping but the digit branch still yields `_1st`, an unexported struct field that the alias-based MarshalJSON/UnmarshalJSON (go/pkg/models/pet.go:114-125) skips, so the property is silently dropped in both directions. csharp also gets `_1st`, which its own comment says CA1707 rejects under the analyzers. A property or query parameter such as `2fa` or `1stPlace` therefore produces six different results.
findings.suspected_forced_reason: None. Digit-leading names need a separate prefix path from keyword escaping.

findings.title: Model-name collisions with built-in or SDK types are guarded only in node (e.g. a schema named Error breaks swift)
findings.description: AbstractBetterCodegen.toModelName applies a collision prefix only when getModelNameCollisionPrefix() is non-empty and the PascalCase name is in languageSpecificPrimitives. Only node sets a prefix ("Model"). In the other 11, a schema named `Error` shadows `Swift.Error` across the whole PetstoreClient module. The SDK itself uses it unqualified (DefaultApiClient.swift:723 `private struct UndecodableBody: Error`, SerializationError.swift:19 `cause: Error?`), so swift stops compiling. Likewise, schemas named `String` or `Object` shadow java.lang types inside the java and kotlin models package. php forbids `String` as a class name. rust model files `use super::*`, so a model named `Result` or `String` shadows the prelude. `Error`, `Date` and `Result` are common schema names. Only node renames the colliding model.
findings.suspected_forced_reason: None

findings.title: Numeric default literals compile in java only: kotlin/csharp/rust/node/python emit literals that do not type-check, or corrupt them
findings.description: java's toDefaultValue adds the `L` and `F` suffixes and wraps a format-less number or decimal in `new java.math.BigDecimal("...")`. The other SDKs emit the raw default verbatim, with these results. kotlin maps number to BigDecimal and float to Float, so `val x: BigDecimal? = 1.5` and `val f: Float? = 1.5` do not compile. csharp maps number to decimal and float to float, so `decimal? X = 1.5` is CS0664 (needs the `M` suffix) and float needs `f`. rust maps number to f64, so an integral default `3` gives `Some(3)` in an Option<f64>, error E0308. node maps a format-less number to the branded `Decimal` string type, so `x: Decimal = 1.5` is a TS type error. python's fixEnumDefaultValue override has no isEnum guard: it prefixes the class name onto any default containing `.` that is not a quoted string, so `default: 1.5` becomes `Defaults1.5`, which is invalid Python (the base implementation and php both check prop.isEnum). The only petstore defaults are `retries: 3` (int32) and enum or string values, so none of this is exercised.

evidence.quote: Numeric/boolean defaults render verbatim as TypeScript literals.
if (prop.defaultValue != null && prop.defaultValue.contains(".") && !prop.defaultValue.startsWith("'") ... prop.defaultValue = model.classname + prop.defaultValue;

findings.suspected_forced_reason: None. Each is a literal-formatting omission that java already handles.

findings.title: format: uri is a validated typed URI in 6 SDKs and an unvalidated plain string in 6, despite stdlib URI types existing
findings.description: The typeMapping for URI differs across the 12, and so does what each SDK accepts for Pet.homepageUrl. java maps it to java.net.URI, which rejects malformed syntax on decode. kotlin uses io.ktor.http.Url, which is lenient. csharp uses System.Uri. php uses Uri\Rfc3986\Uri, and UriNormalizer throws on an invalid value. python uses UrlStr, an HttpUrl validator that also rejects relative and non-http(s) URIs such as `mailto:x` or `/a`. node uses a type-only brand with no runtime check. dart, swift, go, ruby, rust and elixir keep a plain String and accept anything. The golden shows the split: java Pet.java:124 `URI`, kotlin Pet.kt:80 `Url`, csharp Pet.cs:161 `Uri`, php Pet.php:58 `\Uri\Rfc3986\Uri`, python pet.py:46 `UrlStr`, node pet.ts:60 `URI`, versus dart pet.dart:66, go pet.go:75, ruby pet.rbs:14, rust pet.rs:50, swift Pet.swift:33 and elixir pet.ex:25, all String. dart (`Uri`), swift (`URL`), go (`net/url`), ruby (`URI`) and elixir (`URI`) all have stdlib URI types, so no language feature forces the split, and AGENTS.md does not record it.
findings.suspected_forced_reason: Partly: rust has no stdlib URL type (the url crate is external). The other five string-typed SDKs have stdlib types.

findings.title: Operation-level server URLs and server-variable enum values are HTML-escaped in all 12 SDKs, which changes bytes on the wire; global servers emit them raw
findings.description:
Every operation-server template writes the URL literal as `"{{url}}"` and each server-variable enum constant as `"{{value}}"`, both double-brace and therefore HTML-escaped. The global server path writes `{{{serverUrl}}}` and `{{{.}}}` raw in all 12.

An operation server such as `https://h.example.com/v1?api-version=2024-01-01` therefore compiles to `https://h.example.com/v1?api-version=2024-01-01`. I confirmed this by rendering the java fragment. Any `&`, `'` or `=` in an operation-server URL or enum value is corrupted on the wire, identically in all 12 languages, while the same URL declared as a global server is sent correctly. The current goldens are unaffected only because the fixture URLs contain no such characters.
findings.suspected_forced_reason: None.

findings.title: Package-manifest description is escaped differently per language: entity-encoded in 4 manifests, raw XML or raw strings in others
findings.description:
appDescription (escapeText'd info.description) reaches the published package metadata in three different ways:
- HTML-escaped `{{appDescription}}`: node package.json, php composer.json, python pyproject.toml, rust Cargo.toml. A description like `Pets & owners' API` is published to npm, Packagist, PyPI and crates.io as `Pets & owners' API`.
- Raw into XML: java pom.xml `<description>{{{appDescription}}}</description>` and csharp csproj `<Description>{{{appDescription}}}</Description>`. A `&` or `<` makes the XML ill-formed, so the Maven and MSBuild builds fail.
- Raw into a string literal: ruby gemspec `'...'` (an apostrophe is a syntax error, and the escapeText `\"` stays a literal backslash), kotlin `"..."` (`$` interpolates), elixir `"..."` (`#{` interpolates), and dart pubspec as an unquoted YAML scalar (`: `, a leading `&`/`*`/`#` breaks parsing, and `\"` stays literal).

The same info.description thus yields correct, entity-garbled or unbuildable package metadata depending on the language.

evidence.quote: <description>A simplified Pet Store API for integration testing.</description>

findings.suspected_forced_reason: Each manifest format needs its own escaping, but none of these templates applies it.

findings.title: Raw tag and externalDocs prose skips escapeText, so a multi-line or '*/' description breaks compilation in some SDKs but not others
findings.description:
injectTagMetadata stores `tag.getDescription()` and the tag externalDocs description raw. Model and operation externalDocs are raw ExternalDocumentation objects. None of them pass through escapeText, so newlines are not collapsed and the `*/` to `*_/` guard in AbstractBetterCodegen.escapeUnsafeCharacters never runs on them.

What breaks depends on the comment style:
- A multi-line tag description (a common `description: |` block) lands as `// line1\nline2` or `/// line1\nline2`. The second line is bare code, so go, rust, swift, dart and csharp fail to compile, and ruby (`# `) fails too.
- java, kotlin, php and node survive the newline inside `/** */`, but a `*/` in the same raw text closes their block comment early.
- python and elixir place it in `"""` docstrings or heredocs, where only a literal `"""` or (in elixir) `#{` breaks.

The same spec text therefore compiles in some SDKs and not in others. I rendered go's `{{#tagDescription}}\n// {{.}}` with a two-line value and got an uncommented second line.
findings.suspected_forced_reason: None. Operation notes and model descriptions are already normalised through escapeText.

findings.title: Spec prose is HTML-escaped by {{...}} in 5 languages' API docs and left raw by {{{...}}} in the other 7, for the same doc slot
findings.description:
The main templates go through openapi-generator's MustacheEngineAdapter. It uses jmustache's default compiler, and AbstractBetterCodegen does not override processCompiler, so `{{x}}` HTML-escapes its value while `{{{x}}}` emits it raw. I checked this with jmustache 1.16: `pet's "x" a<b & c=d` renders as `pet's "x" a<b & c=d`. Only renderOptionsTemplate sets escapeHTML(false).

The 12 API templates disagree on which form they use for the same spec-prose slots:
- Operation parameter description and per-parameter example summary/description: escaped in node, dart, go, rust and swift; raw in java, kotlin, csharp (escapeXml), php, python, ruby and elixir.
- Tag description and tag/operation externalDocs description: escaped in node, go, rust and swift (dart escapes only the tag description); raw in the others.
- Operation-server variant description: escaped only in go.
- Model externalDocs description and model plural-example summary/description: escaped in all 12. csharp model.mustache:421/649 escapes twice (`{{summary}}` inside `lambda.escapeXml`), so `&` reaches the docs as a literal `&` inside CDATA.

Result: a parameter described as `the pet's "nickname"` renders as `pet's \"nickname\"` in node/dart/go/rust/swift and as `pet's \"nickname\"` in the other 7. The named-entity part (`"`, `&`, `<`) fails generatedCodeShouldNotContainHtmlEntities in those 5 languages only. This undoes AbstractBetterCodegen.preprocessOpenAPI, which decodes `"` from buf/protoc specs precisely so it does not reach generated docs. The petstore golden is clean only because no parameter, tag or externalDocs prose contains `' " & < > = \``.

evidence.quote: // {{description}}   (op-server variant; dart:44, rust:51, swift:25, java:84 use {{{description}}})
* @param petId ID of pet to return (required)
// param petId: ID of pet to return
* @param petId ID of pet to return (required)

findings.suspected_forced_reason: None. The comment syntax is the same kind of prose slot in every language, and 7 languages already use triple braces there.

findings.title: String default literals are escaped ad hoc per language: ruby/php keep stray backslashes, four SDKs break on an apostrophe, and python skips escapeText
findings.description:
toDefaultValue for a string schema is written separately in each codegen:
- ruby, dart and php use `"'" + escapeText(default) + "'"`; node uses `getQuoteChar() + escapeText(...) + getQuoteChar()`.
- java, kotlin, go, rust, swift, csharp and elixir use `"\"" + escapeText(...) + "\""`.
- python uses `"'" + val.replace("'", "\\'") + "'"`, with no escapeText at all.

Because escapeText escapes `"` and `\` but not `'`, the results differ:
1. A default containing `'` is a syntax error in ruby, dart, php and node, but fine in python and the 7 double-quote languages.
2. A default containing `"` becomes `\"`. In ruby and php single-quoted strings that backslash is literal (verified: ruby `'a\"b'.length == 4`), so the in-memory default, and the serialized wire value, is `say \"hi\"` instead of `say "hi"`. node, dart and python decode it correctly.
3. python alone keeps raw newlines (syntax error) and undoubled backslashes (`\n` becomes a real newline), because it bypasses escapeText.
4. kotlin `"$USD"` and dart `'$USD'` interpolate.
findings.suspected_forced_reason: None.

findings.title: escapeUnsafeCharacters overrides do not match each language's real hazards: python's rule is dead, ruby's leaks '\#{' into comments, and elixir has no '#{' guard
findings.description:
python: the override replaces `'''` because Python 'uses triple-quote docstrings', but every python template docstring is `"""` (api.mustache:52,102; model.mustache), and escapeText has already turned `"` into `\"`. The rule never protects anything; it only rewrites `'''` in prose to `'_'_'`.

ruby: the override rewrites `#{` to `\#{` (and `=begin`/`=end`) for every escapeText'd string. ruby renders those strings in `#` comments and single-quoted literals, where `#{` is inert, so `\#{` leaks into the docs. unescapeDocComment only reverses `\"` and `\\`.

elixir: it actually interpolates `#{...}` inside `"..."` and `"""` heredocs, and puts escapeText'd prose straight into `@moduledoc "{{{description}}}"` and `@doc """ {{{summary}}} {{{.}}} """`. Yet it inherits only the base `*/` rule. An operation description like `Fetches /users/#{id}` compiles in the other 11 SDKs but breaks elixir (undefined variable `id` under --warnings-as-errors) or silently interpolates.
findings.suspected_forced_reason: Each language does need its own rule, but the current rules target the wrong hazards: python's and ruby's are dead or harmful, and elixir's is missing.

findings.title: rustdoc and javadocDescription doc-safety lambdas cover only model and property descriptions; operation, tag, parameter and server prose can fail the doc gates
findings.description:
rust: BetterRustCodegen registers `rustdoc` to escape `< > [ ]` because `RUSTDOCFLAGS="-D warnings" cargo doc` (RustLintingSpec) otherwise fails on an unclosed HTML tag or an unresolved intra-doc link. It is used only at rust/models/model.mustache:20 and :137. Operation summary and notes (api.mustache:99,102), tag description (80), parameter description (112), plural examples (115-116, model 143-144), server variant description (51), externalDocs (61, 83, 108) and servers.mustache:37 are unwrapped. An operation description such as `Returns [items] for <admin>` therefore fails rust's lint gate while the same text in a model description passes.

java: `javadocDescription` (doclint=all, checkstyle) wraps only model.mustache:671 (property). Class-level model descriptions, operation summary and notes, tag description and server variant descriptions are unwrapped.

csharp: escapeXml is applied thoroughly in api/model, but not at servers.mustache:26/28 (raw `{{{serverUrl}}}` / `{{{serverDescription}}}` inside `<summary>`), where `&` or `<` raises CS1570 under --warnaserror.
findings.suspected_forced_reason: None. The lambdas exist precisely for this and are simply not applied at these sites.

findings.title: README tooling sections describe linters and rulesets that the shipped configs do not use (java, kotlin, csharp, php, go, dart, swift)
findings.description: Several READMEs describe tooling that the generated project does not have. java points to a '`checkstyle.xml` at project root'; none is generated, and the pom uses the bundled `/google_checks.xml` plus checkstyle-suppressions.xml. kotlin says 'ships with three configured tools' and lists two. csharp lists `StyleCop.Analyzers` as the linter and says 'Run Roslyn / StyleCop analyzers', but the csproj comment says StyleCop.Analyzers was dropped. php claims PHP-CS-Fixer uses 'PHP84Migration + PHP82Migration:risky' and phpcs uses 'PSR-12 + SlevomatCodingStandard'; .php-cs-fixer.dist.php sets only `@PSR12` and phpcs.xml references only PSR12. php also omits the EARLY_RETURN rector set that rector.php enables. go says golangci-lint 'bundles/runs staticcheck, revive, gocritic, gosec, bodyclose', but .golangci.yml is bare `version: "2"`. dart lists 'Strict rules via `package:very_good_analysis`'; that package is neither in pubspec dev_dependencies nor included in analysis_options.yaml. swift's README table lists `NeverForceUnwrap` and `NeverUseForceTry` among the rules the generated code cannot satisfy, but .swift-format enables both (`true`). The other five READMEs (python, ruby, node, rust, elixir) describe their configs accurately.

evidence.quote: The SDK ships with three configured tools:
# Lint (runs staticcheck, revive, gocritic, gosec, bodyclose, errcheck, ...)
| `NeverForceUnwrap`, `NeverUseForceTry` | Test code asserts on values the fixture guarantees

findings.suspected_forced_reason: None. The README templates drifted from the config templates.

findings.title: SKILLS 'Binary / File Uploads' states the wrong upload parameter type in java, kotlin, php and go
findings.description: Each SKILLS file states the type that file-upload parameters take. Four of them do not match the generated Options classes. java says `File`, but the options take `java.io.InputStream` (`List<InputStream>` for multi-file). kotlin says `java.io.File`, but the field is `ByteArray`. php says `SplFileInfo`, but the parameter is `\SplFileObject`, a subclass, so passing a plain SplFileInfo is a TypeError. go says `io.Reader`, but the field is `*os.File`. The other 8 (csharp Stream, python bytes, ruby IO, node Buffer, dart Uint8List, rust Vec<u8>, swift Data, elixir binary()) match their code. An agent following these four docs writes code that does not compile.

evidence.quote: File upload parameters are typed as `File`.
File upload parameters are typed as `java.io.File`.
File upload parameters are typed as `SplFileInfo`.
File upload parameters are typed as `io.Reader`.

findings.suspected_forced_reason: None. These are hardcoded template strings that do not match the codegen type mapping.

findings.title: kotlin README and Makefile run `./gradlew`, but no Gradle wrapper is generated; README's 'Gradle toolchain pins to 17' JVM floor is not enforced
findings.description: The kotlin README (Build, Test, Lint) and every Makefile target invoke `./gradlew`. The golden ships no `gradlew`, `gradlew.bat` or `gradle/wrapper/`, so every documented command fails with 'no such file'. The spec itself runs plain `gradle` (KotlinBuildSpec). The README Requirements also says 'JVM 17 or newer (Gradle toolchain pins to 17)'. build.gradle.kts sets no `jvmToolchain` and no compile `jvmTarget`, and its own comment says 'Use whatever JDK is on PATH ... we skip that'; only detekt sets jvmTarget=17. This breaks the R6-1 rule that the README floor must track what the manifest enforces. The JVM floor also differs from the sibling JVM SDK: java requires 21 (`<release>21</release>`). No language feature forces that split.

evidence.quote: // Use whatever JDK is on PATH ... Toolchain auto-provisioning requires extra repos configured; we skip that.

findings.suspected_forced_reason: None.

findings.title: node README says edge runtimes throw 'a typed `ApiError`' for proxy/CA/TLS-off; the code throws a built-in TypeError
findings.description: The node README 'Runtime support' section says that requesting proxy, custom-CA or TLS-off on Deno, Bun or edge runtimes 'throws a typed `ApiError`'. The portable transport actually throws `new TypeError(...)` (default-api-client.web.ts:53, with its own JSDoc `@throws TypeError`). That is the correct behaviour under the AGENTS error contract (a caller mistake raises the language built-in, never ApiError), and it mirrors dart's README, which correctly says ArgumentError. The README misdocuments the error type users should catch.

evidence.quote: standard Fetch API there, so requesting one throws a typed `ApiError` rather
requesting one throws an `ArgumentError` at construction

findings.suspected_forced_reason: None.

findings.title: node SKILLS.md imports every symbol from `./src/...` paths a consumer cannot reach; the other 11 import from the published package
findings.description: Every TypeScript example in node/SKILLS.md imports from a relative source path, for example `import { Client } from "./src/client.js"`, `./src/auth/bearer-authenticator.js` and `./src/errors/not-found-error.js`. After `npm install petstore-client`, which the same file recommends, these paths do not exist in the consumer's project. package.json `exports` exposes only `.` and `./package.json`, and the barrel src/index.ts says that everything else under src/ 'is internal plumbing and must not be imported by consumers'. The barrel already exports Client, the authenticators, TransportOptions, Servers, the errors and the models. Every other SDK's SKILLS imports from its published package namespace (com.example.petstore.*, petstore_client.*, PetstoreClient\*, package:petstore_client, petstore::...).

evidence.quote: everything else under `src/` ... is internal plumbing and must not be imported by consumers.

findings.suspected_forced_reason: None. The examples should import from the package entry point.

findings.title: ruby: blank lines inside the generated YARD block detach the operation summary and @param tags from the method
findings.description: In ruby/api/api.mustache the options @param is wrapped in the non-standalone line `{{#vendorExtensions.op.signatureArgs}}{{#isOptions}}` (template lines 102-104), which emits an empty `` line before and after `# @param options`. YARD builds a docstring only from the contiguous `#` block directly above a `def`, and a blank line ends that block. Only the trailing `@return/@raise/@deprecated/@see` lines reach the method. The summary ('Add a new pet to the store'), the body/path `@param` tags and the options `@param` are dropped from the docs that `make docs` (`yard doc --fail-on-warning`, with .yardopts shipped) produces. Every operation is affected. The other 11 SDKs keep the summary and parameters in the attached doc comment.

evidence.quote:
# Add a new pet to the store
# @param pet [Pet] Create a new pet in the store

# @param options [AddPetOptions] ...

# @return [Pet]

findings.suspected_forced_reason: None. It is mustache standalone-line whitespace.

findings.title: swift README decimal caveat recommends a non-existent API (`JSONDecoder().userInfo[.useDecimal]`); AGENTS.md repeats the false claim
findings.description: The swift README tells users who need exact decimals to decode 'with `JSONDecoder().userInfo[.useDecimal] = true`'. Foundation has no such CodingUserInfoKey. A compile check with the local toolchain (`swiftc -typecheck`) fails with: type 'CodingUserInfoKey' has no member 'useDecimal'. The real opt-in is to decode into a `Decimal`-typed field. CLAUDE.md requires every example to compile when pasted verbatim. AGENTS.md (forced-divergence entry for `format: number`) cites the same non-existent opt-in as the documented caller workaround.

evidence.quote: Foundation's `JSONDecoder` decodes JSON numbers into `Double` (opt in with `userInfo[.useDecimal]`)

findings.suspected_forced_reason: None.

findings.title: Dart and Go spec setup rewrites the golden before the checks run, so the dart format gate cannot fail and go.mod/go.sum drift is hidden
findings.description: SharedRuntimeContainer runs getSetupCommands() inside /work and then snapshots the result (`cp -a /work /work-snapshot`, SharedRuntimeContainer.java:223). Every spec method restores that snapshot, not the committed golden. DartSpec's setup ends with `dart fix --apply ...` and then `dart format .`, so DartFormattingSpec's `dart format --set-exit-if-changed .` always runs on a tree that was formatted a moment earlier. It cannot fail, and formatting drift in the committed dart golden is never caught. GoSpec's setup runs `go mod tidy`, which rewrites go.mod/go.sum before GoBuildSpec, GoLintingSpec, GoClientSpec and GoWasmSpec, so an untidy manifest or a missing go.sum entry is hidden. A client's `make build` (`go build ./...`) has no tidy step and would hit that error. No other language's setup modifies sources or manifests; their setup only installs dependencies. This contradicts the AGENTS.md 'Known-thin gates' claim that every check runs 'in check mode ... no write-mode-posing-as-check'. The DartSpec setup comment is also stale: it says '770 info-level findings remain ... they don't fail the spec', but DartLintingSpec runs `dart analyze --fatal-warnings --fatal-infos`. The setup's `dart fix` codes (always_use_package_imports, directives_ordering, document_ignores) are not enabled by `include: package:lints/recommended.yaml`, so that step does nothing.

evidence.quote: (770 info-level findings remain, all from rules without safe fix producers — they don't fail the spec)
every language's lint/format/type-check runs in **check mode** ... no write-mode-posing-as-check

findings.suspected_forced_reason: None. The generator already runs dart format and go mod tidy at generation time, so the golden should pass without these setup steps; the checks should run on the committed tree.

findings.title: Every SDK ships a warnings-fatal docs build, but only rust runs it in a spec
findings.description: Each generated Makefile has a `docs` target meant to fail on documentation warnings: java javadoc `-DfailOnWarnings=true -Ddoclint=all`, kotlin dokka `failOnWarning.set(true)`, csharp docfx `--warningsAsErrors`, php phpDocumentor plus a log grep, python `sphinx-build -W`, ruby `yard doc --fail-on-warning`, node `typedoc --treatWarningsAsErrors`, dart `dart doc --validate-links` plus a warning grep, swift docc `--warnings-as-errors`, elixir `mix docs --warnings-as-errors`. RustLintingSpec is the only spec that runs one (`RUSTDOCFLAGS="-D warnings" cargo doc`). A grep of src/spec/java finds no javadoc, dokka, docfx, sphinx, yard, typedoc, dart doc, generate-documentation or mix docs invocation. A broken doc reference in the other 10 SDKs fails nothing in CI and only shows up in a client's `make docs`. go's docs target (gomarkdoc) has no warnings-fatal mode and is not run either.

findings.title: Five SDKs' decompression integration tests call a public internet host and pass whether or not the body was encoded
findings.description: java, kotlin, csharp, php, rust and elixir run their 'decompresses gzip/brotli/zstd response' integration tests against the chasm fixture's `/test/compressed/<enc>` endpoints. The fixture's `x-chasm-content-encoding` makes it really send that encoding, so asserting on the body proves the client decoded it. ruby, python, node, go and dart send the same three tests to `https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts/1` and assert only status 200 and that the body contains 'userId'. Nothing makes that server use the requested encoding: an identity response passes, so the tests do not show that the br/zstd/gzip decode path ran. The tests also depend on the public internet and a third-party host (node's own comment adds a 30s timeout 'because jsonplaceholder.typicode.com is an external host'), so CI can be flaky or blocked offline. The chasm endpoints are already in every SDK's fixture openapi.yaml.

evidence.quote: // 30s timeout because jsonplaceholder.typicode.com is an external host

findings.title: Generated tests get weaker compile and analysis strictness than sources in swift, csharp and java
findings.description: AGENTS.md says linters and type checkers run 'over sources **and** tests'. Most languages apply the same strictness to tests (rust clippy --all-targets -D warnings, go vet/staticcheck ./..., dart analyze --fatal-infos, node tsc -p tsconfig.jest.json, php phpstan level 9 over `.`, kotlin detekt over src/test). Three do not. (1) swift: Package.swift puts `-warnings-as-errors` only on the PetstoreClient library target. The PetstoreClientTests testTarget has no swiftSettings, and SwiftLintingSpec runs a plain `swift build` (sources only), leaving the tests to `swift test`, so test-code warnings are never fatal. This is not forced: the same `-Wwarning DeprecatedDeclaration` downgrade the library uses would work for the tests. (2) csharp: CSharpStaticAnalysisSpec builds PetstoreClient.Test.csproj with `--warnaserror`, but that project sets none of AnalysisLevel=latest-all, AnalysisMode=All or EnforceCodeStyleInBuild (the SDK csproj sets all three). The test code is therefore checked only against the default analyzer set, while the SDK gets every CA rule. (3) java: spotbugs-maven-plugin defaults to includeTests=false and the pom does not override it, so SpotBugs never sees src/test, though checkstyle sets includeTestSourceDirectory=true. (elixir's `mix test` also runs without --warnings-as-errors. The ElixirClientSpec comment gives a reason: deprecation warnings at call sites cannot be suppressed in elixir. That is borderline-forced and not recorded in AGENTS.md.)

evidence.quote: The test target is type-checked by SwiftClientSpec's `swift test`

findings.suspected_forced_reason: None for swift, csharp or java. elixir's test exemption is borderline (no per-call deprecation suppression).

findings.title: Hand-written spec tests in the generated spec/ directory never run in kotlin, swift, php and python
findings.description: AbstractBetterCodegen.getSpecDir() documents a directory 'where user-written spec tests should be placed', and every SDK gets one. In java (build-helper add-test-source plus a failsafe `**/*Spec.java` include), csharp (the root test csproj globs Spec/**), ruby (Rakefile pattern spec/**/*_spec.rb), node (jest testMatch `**/spec/**/*.spec.ts`), go (`./...`), dart (test/spec) and elixir (test/spec), files placed there are compiled and run. In four languages they are not. kotlin: `src/spec/kotlin` is in no KMP sourceSet (jvmTest is only src/test/kotlin) and not in detekt's source list, so it is never compiled, run or linted. swift: Package.swift excludes `Spec` from the only test target. php: phpunit.xml's single testsuite is `<directory suffix="Test.php">tests</directory>`, and composer autoload-dev maps only tests/. python: pyproject sets `testpaths = ["test", "spec"]`, but both PythonClientSpec and the generated Makefile run `python -m pytest test/ -v`, and the explicit path overrides testpaths, so spec/ is skipped. mypy also checks only `petstore_client/ test/`. A client's hand-written specs in these four SDKs pass silently because nothing runs them.

findings.title: Inline-comment ban is switched off for kotlin and rust, and csharp's /Models/ exclusion hides a real violation
findings.description: AbstractFormattingSpec.generatedCodeShouldNotContainInlineComments bans `//` line comments in generated source. java, csharp, php, node, dart and swift enforce it, and the java/kotlin/dart/swift templates use `/* */` instead. KotlinFormattingSpec and RustFormattingSpec return null from getInlineCommentPattern(), which skips the check. Neither language is forced: both have separate doc-comment syntax (KDoc `/** */`, rust `///`/`//!`) and block comments, so the dart/swift pattern `^\s*//($|[^/])` would work. Simulating the spec's own logic (file header skipped) finds 406 `//` comments in 20 files under kotlin/src/main (e.g. DefaultApiClient.kt:175 from templates/kotlin/default_api_client.mustache:169) and 1179 under rust/src (e.g. transport_options.rs:183 from templates/rust/transport_options.mustache:178). java/src/main, swift/Sources, dart/lib, node/src and php/lib all have 0. CSharpFormattingSpec also excludes every path containing `/Models/`. The only violation that exclusion hides is `// Gap AX.1 — OAS 3.1 ...` in Models/StrictTag.cs:21 (templates/csharp/models/model.mustache:504 and :674). java, kotlin, dart and swift render the same comment as `/* */`. (go, python, ruby and elixir are fairly exempt: `#` is their only comment syntax, or `//` is the godoc doc-comment syntax.)

findings.title: java's OpenRewrite modernization recipe is never run by any spec, though the pom relies on it and php gates its rector equivalent
findings.description: The java pom disables `-Xlint:deprecation` and says deprecated JDK/library API use 'is instead caught by the OpenRewrite UpgradeToJava25 recipe configured below'. That recipe is bound to no lifecycle phase. It is reachable only through the Makefile's write-mode `upgrade` target (`mvn rewrite:run`), and no java spec runs `rewrite:dryRun`: JavaStaticAnalysisSpec runs only `spotbugs:check checkstyle:check`. So the deprecation check the pom says replaces -Xlint is not enforced. php has the same kind of tool (rector `LevelSetList::UP_TO_PHP_84`) and gates it with PhpModernizationSpec (`rector process --dry-run`). The code contradicts its own comment, and java is weaker than php here.

findings.title: Form-body (x-www-form-urlencoded) encoding differs: java, ruby and node use the WHATWG set (* literal, ~ escaped); the other 8 do the opposite
findings.description: For setPetPreferences the form body is encoded with two different character sets. java (URLEncoder), ruby (URI.encode_www_form) and node (URLSearchParams) keep `*` literal and escape `~` as %7E. csharp (EscapeDataString with %20→+), php (rawurlencode with %20→+), python (urlencode/quote_plus), dart (Uri.encodeQueryComponent), go (url.Values.Encode), rust (form_url_encode), swift (CharacterSet `-._~`) and elixir (URI.encode_www_form) do the reverse. Kotlin is broken separately (first finding). For nickname="a~b*c", confirmed with runtime encoders: java/ruby/node send `nickname=a%7Eb*c` and the rest send `nickname=a~b%2Ac`. Both are valid form encodings, but the bytes differ, and the rust helper's comment says the escape set is meant to be identical across every SDK.
findings.suspected_forced_reason: none; each stdlib form encoder can be post-processed the same way the query encoders already are

findings.title: JSON request bodies are escaped differently: php and swift escape / as \/, php also escapes non-ASCII as \uXXXX
findings.description: Most SDKs write `/` and non-ASCII characters as-is in JSON request bodies (verified: java, kotlin, python, ruby, node, dart, rust, elixir). php calls `json_encode($sanitized, $flags)` with flags 0, so it sends every `/` as `\/` and every non-ASCII character as `\uXXXX`: Pet{name:"café", photoUrls:["https://x/y.png"]} becomes `"café"` and `"https:\/\/x\/y.png"`. swift's JSONEncoder and JSONSerialization are configured without `.withoutEscapingSlashes`, so every photoUrls value and every base64 `format: byte` value containing `/` goes out as `\/` (confirmed with swift on macOS: `{"name":"café\/ü","photoUrls":["https:\/\/x\/y.png"]}`). swift's own test locks this in (ObjectSerializerTests.swift:985-989). Two smaller cases: go's encoding/json always escapes U+2028 and U+2029, even with SetEscapeHTML(false). csharp's `JavaScriptEncoder.UnsafeRelaxedJsonEscaping` still writes characters outside the Basic Multilingual Plane (emoji) as `😀` pairs, based on known .NET behaviour (I could not run .NET here). Every body-carrying operation is affected (addPet, updatePet, placeOrder, setPetAvatarThumbnail, …). AGENTS records that go's HTML-escaping was turned off so bytes go out literally "like every other SDK"; php and swift break that same rule. Fix: php `JSON_UNESCAPED_SLASHES | JSON_UNESCAPED_UNICODE`; swift `outputFormatting = .withoutEscapingSlashes` and `options: .withoutEscapingSlashes`.
findings.suspected_forced_reason: php/swift: none (flags exist). go U+2028/2029 and csharp supplementary-plane escaping are stdlib behaviours that would need a custom writer; borderline
findings.note: done in php; still open for csharp, go, swift

php.note: Same root cause as F038 (php json_encode flags). The swift, go and csharp parts are outside this scope.

findings.title: Query-value encoding differs in 2 languages: java escapes ~ but not *; node keeps ! * ' ( ) ~ literal
findings.description: Nine SDKs encode non-allowReserved query keys and values with the RFC 3986 unreserved set `A-Za-z0-9-._~`: csharp, php, python, ruby, dart, go, rust, swift, elixir. Kotlin is broken separately (previous finding). Two others differ on the same input. java uses `URLEncoder.encode(...).replace("+","%20")`, which escapes `~` as %7E and keeps `*` literal. node uses `encodeURIComponent`, which keeps `! * ' ( ) ~` literal; fetch's WHATWG URL parser then escapes `'` back to %27. For getPetByName(category="a~b*c!d'e(f)g"), confirmed against runtime encoders: python/elixir/ruby send `a~b%2Ac%21d%27e%28f%29g`, java sends `a%7Eb*c%21d%27e%28f%29g`, node sends `a~b*c!d%27e(f)g`. java already restores `%7E`→`~` in its path and allowReserved encoders (ValueSerializer.java:123, :183). PetApiTest.java:533-544 asserts that `~` must never become %7E, but only on the path. The plain query encoder was never aligned. node's own path encoder (value-serializer.ts:211-224) shows the intended canonical set. This is not covered by the R8-10 OAuth note, which is about the token, Basic and authorize paths only.
findings.suspected_forced_reason: none; java already post-processes URLEncoder output elsewhere, and node already post-processes encodeURIComponent in encodePathSegment

findings.title: dart: a multipart array of strings sends only its last element
findings.description: dart's multipart builder handles a non-binary List field by calling `_addMultipartField` once per element. For a String element that runs `request.fields[name] = value`, and `http.MultipartRequest.fields` is a Map, so each element overwrites the previous one and only the last survives. The code comment says the list "expands into one part per element (repeated keys, as for the urlencoded form)", which is what java (DefaultApiClient.java:888), python (default_api_client.py:868), node, go, rust, swift, ruby, php, csharp, kotlin and elixir actually do. The same happens for num/bool elements (`request.fields[name] = value.toString()`). This is latent in the petstore, which has no multipart string array (`files` is binary and goes through `request.files.add`), but any spec with a multipart array of scalars loses data silently.

findings.title: ruby: Faraday decodes and re-encodes the query string, which undoes allowReserved, sorts parameters and drops repeated keys
findings.description: Ruby builds the query string itself in base_api.rb `build_query_string`, then passes the full URL to `Faraday::Connection#run_request`. Faraday's `Request#url` parses that query with the connection's params_encoder (`QueryParamsEncoder.decode` → `NestedParamsEncoder.decode`), and `build_exclusive_url` re-encodes it with `NestedParamsEncoder.encode` plus `Utils.escape` (ESCAPE_RE `/[^a-zA-Z0-9 .~_-]/`). I ran the installed faraday-2.14.2 encoder on a query matching the golden output. (1) allowReserved is undone: `revision=v1.0/beta:rc1` goes out as `revision=v1.0%2Fbeta%3Arc1`, while all other SDKs send `/` and `:` literally (the petstore's own documented example). (2) Every query is reordered alphabetically (`@sort_params = true`), and deepObject sub-keys are sorted as well. (3) Repeated keys collapse to the last value (`m=1&m=2` → `m=2`), so any exploded array query parameter (OAS default style form, explode true) loses all but its last element. The petstore has no exploded query array, so (3) is latent. Ruby's only allowReserved test is the unit test of `encode_query_allowing_reserved` (value_serializer_test.rb:477); no ruby test checks the URL that Faraday actually sends. The QueryParamsEncoder was added only to turn `+` back into %20, and its comment wrongly says it leaves every other character as Faraday encodes it. Fix: pass params separately, or give the encoder an identity decode/encode that keeps the pre-built query unchanged.
findings.suspected_forced_reason: none; Faraday accepts a custom params_encoder whose decode/encode can pass the query through unchanged

ruby.note: Same root cause and fix as F005; the encoder's old comment claiming only spaces change is replaced.

findings.title: AGENTS claims node and python preserve full decimal precision for `type: number`, but both decode weightKg through a binary float; both also accept a quoted string
findings.description: AGENTS.md:246 lists node ('branded Decimal + JSON.rawJSON') and python ('Decimal') among the FIVE precision-preserving SDKs. That holds only on encode. On decode, node's parseJson is a plain JSON.parse, and the constructor then does `String(this.weightKg)`. I checked: 12.34567890123456789 becomes "12.345678901234567", 1.0 becomes "1", and 1e400 becomes "Infinity". python's parse_json is json.loads with the default parse_float=float, so pydantic receives a float. I checked: Decimal('12.345678901234567'). java, kotlin and csharp read the number text exactly (I checked java: 12.34567890123456789). Wire acceptance also diverges: `"weightKg":"1.5"` (quoted) is rejected by java (I checked), kotlin, csharp and the 7 native-float SDKs. python's lax Decimal accepts it, and node accepts ANY string ("abc", "NaN") as the branded Decimal. node's README 'Decimal / format: number precision' section talks only about int64 and never mentions this loss. Fixes: JSON.parse with a reviver using context.source (available in the same runtime that has JSON.rawJSON) and `json.loads(parse_float=Decimal)` or pydantic's lossless JSON path. Otherwise correct AGENTS.

evidence.quote: FIVE preserve full textual precision — java/kotlin (`BigDecimal`), csharp (`decimal`), python (`Decimal`), node (branded `Decimal` + `JSON.rawJSON`)
this.weightKg = String(this.weightKg) as unknown as Decimal;

findings.title: Container/primitive response leaves are lax in python, kotlin and node while model fields are strict (getInventory {"a":"5"} accepted)
findings.description: Applies to getInventory (map<string,int32>), getMatrix ([[int32]]) and StockItem.matrix. python: the return type 'Dict[str, StrictInt]' is mapped through _NATIVE_TYPES_MAPPING 'StrictInt': int to TypeAdapter(dict[str,int]), which is LAX pydantic. findings.title: Fractional/float literal for an integer field: java silently truncates (7.5->7), node keeps 1.5, swift accepts 7.0/1e2; the rest reject
findings.description: Case: Order/Pet `id` (int64) or `quantity` (int32) carrying 1.5, 7.0 or 1e2. java: Jackson's ACCEPT_FLOAT_AS_INT is enabled by default and ALLOW_COERCION_OF_SCALARS does not override it. I checked: `{"quantity":7.5}` gives 7, `{"id":1.5}` gives 1, `{"quantity":1e2}` gives 100, and getInventory `{"a":7.5}` gives {a=7]. That is silent data corruption. node: the model constructor only checks `typeof === 'number'`, so `id: 1.5` is kept verbatim in an integer field. swift: Foundation JSONDecoder accepts exact integral doubles (7.0 and 1e2 decode to 7 and 100, I checked) and rejects 7.5. findings.title: Integer range not enforced on decode in 7 SDKs: int32 3000000000 accepted by swift/python/node/dart/php/ruby/elixir; int64 overflow accepted by python/ruby/elixir
