findings.title: go matches JSON keys case-insensitively: {"ID":7} sets Pet.Id, and {"name":"Rex","NAME":"Evil"} yields Name="Evil"
findings.description: go decodes models via `json.Unmarshal(data, aux)` (encoding/json v1). v1 falls back to a case-insensitive field match when no exact key matches. A response key that differs only in case from a declared property is therefore bound to that field. `{"name":"Rex","photoUrls":[],"ID":7}` gives Id=7 in go, while the other 11 ignore the unknown key and leave id null. With `"name":"Rex","NAME":"Evil"`, go's later case-folded key overwrites, giving Name="Evil" vs "Rex" everywhere else. The Gap AJ required check uses the exact-case raw map, so the presence check and the decoded value can disagree. This is not forced: UnmarshalJSON already builds the raw map and can reject or ignore non-exact keys, or use json/v2 case-sensitive matching.

findings.title: java coerces a JSON number/boolean into a String field ({"name":42} -> "42"); the other 11 reject
findings.description: Jackson's ALLOW_COERCION_OF_SCALARS=false covers only number, boolean and date targets. String (LogicalType.Textual) is excluded, so int->String, float->String and boolean->String coercion stays on. I checked this against jackson-databind 2.19.4 (the golden's version) with the golden mapper config: `{"name":42}` decodes to name="42" and `{"name":true}` to "true". kotlin rejects this and has explicit tests for it (unquotedNumberScalarOnStringFieldThrows). csharp (STJ), go, rust, swift (I checked: typeMismatch), python StrictStr, dart `as String`, php assertPrimitiveTypes, ruby/elixir strict 'String' clauses and node's typeof check all reject it. The java comment claims parity ('Matches the other SDKs, which reject wrong-typed primitives'), but its tests cover only the String->number and number->boolean directions. Fix: `coercionConfigFor(LogicalType.Textual).setCoercion(CoercionInputShape.Integer|Float|Boolean, CoercionAction.Fail)`, plus a test.

findings.title: python accepts the snake_case attribute name as a wire key (populate_by_name=True on decode)
findings.description: Every model sets `ConfigDict(populate_by_name=True)` and responses decode via `klass.model_validate(data)`, so pydantic accepts BOTH the alias and the field name. findings.title: Non-string scalar multipart parts (boolean, date-time, date, $ref enum, uuid) are encoded differently in every SDK. Petstore's multipart scalars are all plain strings
findings.description: The only scalar multipart fields in petstore are `documentType` (an inline enum that every SDK types as String) and `notes`, so the scalar-part encoders are only ever given strings. findings.title: form-urlencoded bodies: ruby skips ObjectSerializer.stringify and nested objects fall back to each language's own string repr. Masked because petstore's form fields are only string/array-of-string/date
findings.description: setPetPreferences is the only x-www-form-urlencoded op. findings.title: The forced-divergence note says python and node preserve full decimal precision; both lose it on decode

findings.title: AGENTS says node and python keep full precision for format:number; python loses it both ways, node on decode
findings.description:
AGENTS.md (Forced divergences) says five SDKs "preserve full textual precision", including python (Decimal) and node (branded Decimal + JSON.rawJSON). The code contradicts this.
- python, decode: ObjectSerializer parses with `json.loads(json_string, parse_constant=...)` and no `parse_float=Decimal`, so the number is already a binary float before pydantic coerces it to Decimal.
- python, encode: the `JsonNumber` alias serializes with `PlainSerializer(lambda value: float(value), when_used="json")`, which narrows to float.
- Verified with pydantic 2.12: `{"w":12.34567890123456789}` decodes to `Decimal('12.345678901234567')`, and `Decimal("12.34567890123456789")` encodes as `12.345678901234567`.
- node, decode: `ObjectSerializer.parseJson` is plain `JSON.parse(json)`, then the model coerces with `String(this.weightKg)`. Verified: `12.345678901234567890` becomes "12.345678901234567" and `12345678901234567890` becomes "12345678901234567000". Only encode is lossless (JSON.rawJSON).

node's README caveat covers int64 only, not Decimal. java, kotlin and csharp really do round-trip losslessly, so the precision-preserving group is three languages, not five. Node can decode losslessly with the reviver `context.source` from the same json-parse-with-source proposal it already relies on for rawJSON. Python can pass `parse_float=Decimal` and emit the raw decimal text. Otherwise AGENTS should list python and node with the lossy group, and their READMEs should carry the caveat.

evidence.quote: FIVE preserve full textual precision — java/kotlin (`BigDecimal`), csharp (`decimal`), python (`Decimal`), node (branded `Decimal` + `JSON.rawJSON`)
this.weightKg = String(this.weightKg) as unknown as Decimal;

findings.title: Configuration and TransportOptions print secrets (proxy password, Authorization default header) in 7 SDKs; every authenticator redacts
findings.description:
The SDK has a redaction policy: every authenticator in all 12 masks its secret in toString, repr, Debug or inspect as `***`. The same secrets also sit in two other public value types. First, the proxy URL holds `user:pass@` credentials by design (python, dart and elixir parse the userinfo into Proxy-Authorization, java pre-computes it, and python's comment says this matches the other 11). Second, the default headers of Configuration and TransportOptions hold credentials: the generated docs use `.defaultHeader("Authorization", "Bearer token")` as the example, and java's PetApiTest does exactly that. Those values print in plain text in 7 languages:
- python: the frozen-dataclass repr prints `proxy='http://user:pass@h'` and the default_headers mapping (verified in /tmp).
- rust: `#[derive(Debug)]` on both structs prints proxy and default_headers; TransportOptions also prints the CA PEM bytes.
- ruby: the default `inspect` dumps the instance variables.
- elixir: the struct `inspect` dumps them, although authenticators use `@derive {Inspect, except: [:token]}`.
- node: `util.inspect` and `console.log` dump the readonly fields, although authenticators define `[nodejs.util.inspect.custom]`.
- php: var_dump and print_r dump the readonly props, although authenticators define `__debugInfo`.
- go: `%+v` prints the defaultHeaders map contents. The proxy is a *url.URL, so only its address prints.
In java, kotlin, csharp, dart and swift the classes have no field-dumping representation (Object, Instance-of, or type-name default), so nothing leaks. Same object, same secret, different logging exposure: either redact (mask proxy userinfo and sensitive header values) in all 12, or never dump in all 12.

evidence.quote: type Configuration struct { baseURL string; defaultHeaders map[string]string }

findings.title: TransportOptions has a public constructor that skips the builder's proxy validation in php, python, ruby and node
findings.description: PARITY_TODO T2-10 says TransportOptions is builder-only "because it has validated invariants": the builder rejects a proxy URL that has no host or does not use http or https. That holds in java (package-private ctor), kotlin (private constructor), csharp (internal ctor), dart (TransportOptions._), swift (fileprivate init), go (unexported fields, Build() returns an error) and rust (private fields, build() returns Result). In php, python, ruby and node the value type has a public constructor that does no checking at all, so the invariant can be skipped. Examples: `new TransportOptions(proxy: 'socks5://h:1080')` (php), `TransportOptions(proxy='ftp://x')` (python, since __post_init__ only wraps the headers), `TransportOptions.new(proxy: 'ftp://x', ...)` (ruby), `new TransportOptions({proxy: 'ftp://x', ...})` (node). Each is accepted, and the bad URL goes straight to Guzzle, urllib3, Faraday or undici. Those libraries then throw their own exceptions or misroute traffic, against the error contract, which says a caller mistake raises the language's built-in error. The same input is rejected up front in the other languages. None of these is forced: php and node can declare a private constructor, ruby can use `private_class_method :new`, and python's frozen dataclass can run the same proxy check in __post_init__. Elixir's `%TransportOptions{}` struct literal is the one forced bypass, since struct literals are always public.

findings.title: Cancellation is impossible in go, csharp and node, which accept no context.Context, CancellationToken or AbortSignal; python's asyncio cancellation leaves the request running. AGENTS' C# cancellation claim is unreachable
findings.description: AGENTS: 'Never rewrap the platform's cancellation ... a cancelled C# request as OperationCanceledException'. In java (Thread.interrupt), kotlin (Job.cancel), swift (Task.cancel), rust (dropping the future) and elixir (killing the process), a caller can abort an in-flight request with the platform's own mechanism. go builds every request with context.Background() and no operation takes a ctx, so a go caller cannot cancel. Every csharp ...Async operation and SendRequestAsync lacks the idiomatic CancellationToken parameter, so a csharp caller cannot cancel. The only test reaches OperationCanceledException through the internal DefaultApiClient(HttpClient) seam plus CancelPendingRequests. node's fetch gets only AbortSignal.timeout and the operations take no signal. python's operations are async def but run the sync urllib3 call through asyncio.to_thread. Cancelling the asyncio task raises CancelledError while the worker thread carries the HTTP request (a POST, say) through to completion. dart Futures are not cancellable and no abort hook is exposed. findings.title: Connection reuse differs: ruby never keeps a connection alive, python's pool holds one connection per host under its concurrent async facade, and go uses a zero-value http.Transport
findings.description: ruby: build_connection uses Faraday's default net_http adapter, which creates a new Net::HTTP per request and wraps it in http.start {...} (faraday-net_http 3.4.x net_http.rb: Net::HTTP.new at :54/:59, http.start at :112). Every ruby request therefore pays a fresh TCP and TLS handshake. The comment claiming the cached connection preserves 'the underlying socket pool / keepalive' is false, and close() has nothing to release. python: urllib3.PoolManager(**kwargs) uses the default maxsize=1 per host, while the async facade runs requests concurrently through asyncio.to_thread. Every concurrent request beyond the first opens a new connection and has it discarded on return, with a 'Connection pool is full' warning. go: buildHTTPClient starts from &http.Transport{} instead of http.DefaultTransport.Clone(). That gives no IdleConnTimeout (idle sockets are held until the server closes them), MaxIdleConnsPerHost=2, no dial or TLS-handshake timeout or TCP keep-alive, and no ProxyFromEnvironment. java, kotlin, csharp, node, rust, swift, php, dart and elixir use pooled keep-alive clients with library-default limits.

findings.title: OIDC rediscovery after the Cache-Control max-age expires throws away the exchanged authorization-code tokens (all 12); discovery is single-flight only in java/go
findings.description: When discoveryExpiry passes (86400 s by default, or whatever max-age the OP sends; max-age=0 makes it immediate), every SDK builds a brand-new OAuth2AuthorizationCodeAuthenticator with tokenExchanged=false and a fresh token manager. The access and refresh tokens from exchangeCode are discarded, and the next getAuthHeaders throws 'Must call exchangeCode() before making API requests' (or its equivalent), which cannot be recovered without a new user authorization. Refreshing the endpoints should carry the token state over. Separately, discovery is serialized only in java (synchronized getDelegate) and go (mutex held across fetch). kotlin/csharp/swift/python/ruby/node/dart/php/elixir fetch outside any lock: concurrent callers fire duplicate discovery requests, and the last writer replaces the delegate, which can silently discard a delegate that exchangeCode just populated. rust instead fails the concurrent caller (separate finding).

findings.title: csharp and dart silently drop a multipart body when replaying it on a 307/308 redirect
findings.description: On 307/308 the original method and body must be replayed. csharp rebuilds the follow-up only for byte[] and string bodies, and throws for Stream. A multipart body (Dictionary<string, object>) matches no branch, so next.Content stays null and the redirected POST goes out with no body. dart likewise copies only Uint8List or String into the follow-up http.Request. A multipart body (Map, sent via http.MultipartRequest) is dropped, while the content headers are kept because nextBody != null. The other 10 replay multipart intact: java's repeatable publisher, kotlin rebuilds through buildRequestBody, rust/python/node/ruby pre-serialize to bytes, go's *bytes.Buffer gets GetBody, swift's URLSession keeps httpBody, and php/elixir re-encode.

findings.title: dart's request timeout does not abort the in-flight request and does not cover the response body read
findings.description: The total deadline is Future.timeout around _httpClient.send(...), which only stops waiting for the response headers. The response body is then read with streamedResponse.stream.toBytes() with no deadline, so a server that sends headers and then stalls the body hangs a dart call forever. dart:io's connectionTimeout covers connect only, and idleTimeout applies to idle pooled connections, not an in-progress read. When the headers timeout fires, the underlying request is not cancelled: the socket stays open and the eventual StreamedResponse is never listened to (leaked). The other SDKs' deadlines abort the request and cover the body: go client.Timeout, node AbortSignal.timeout, rust reqwest timeout, csharp HttpClient.Timeout with buffered content, kotlin request/socket timeouts, swift resource timeout, elixir Task.shutdown, php max_duration, and the python/ruby read timeouts.
findings.suspected_forced_reason: package:http ^1.2 has no abort API. The body read can still be bounded with .timeout(), and the io client can be closed or aborted (newer package:http exposes Abortable requests), so this is not forced.

findings.title: python redirect loop mutates the shared PoolManager.proxy_headers, so concurrent requests race and can lose proxy credentials permanently
findings.description: _follow_redirects snapshots self._pool_manager.proxy_headers, deletes Proxy-Authorization from that shared dict on a cross-origin hop, and restores it in finally. The pool manager is shared by every request on the client, and the async facade runs requests concurrently on worker threads (asyncio.to_thread). While one request is mid-redirect, every other concurrent request through the ProxyManager goes out without Proxy-Authorization and gets a 407. Two overlapping cross-origin redirects corrupt the state for good: A snapshots {PA} and strips it, B snapshots {} (already stripped), A restores {PA}, then B restores {}, and the client loses its proxy credentials for its lifetime. No other SDK mutates shared transport state per request: java/kotlin/csharp/etc. strip Proxy-Authorization from a per-request header copy.

findings.title: swift's production session uses URLSessionConfiguration.default: a process-wide cookie jar and response cache that no other SDK has

A Set-Cookie from any response is stored process-wide and replayed as a Cookie header on later requests from every swift Client in the process (including clients for other tenants or credentials). The other 11 are stateless: csharp explicitly sets UseCookies=false ('The other 11 SDKs are stateless by default'), and none of java/kotlin/go/node/python/ruby/php/rust/dart/elixir installs a cookie jar or cache. findings.title: Query and form parameter order on the wire varies: insertion, hash, random, or sorted
findings.description: For the same call, the 12 SDKs put query params on the wire in different orders. csharp, node, php, dart, kotlin (map side) and rust follow declaration (insertion) order. java collects into a `HashMap`, so the order is the hash order. go ranges over a `map[string]any`, which is randomized per iteration, so the same request can produce a different query each time. swift iterates a `[String: Any?]`, which is randomized per process. ruby is sorted alphabetically by Faraday. elixir is sorted by key (small Erlang maps). python moves every allowReserved param to the end. The Ktor transport also regroups repeated keys. deepObject sub-keys follow each language's map order, which is random in go, rust and swift. Form bodies: go sorts (`url.Values.Encode`), swift is random, java follows HashMap order, the rest use insertion order. The bytes are non-deterministic in go and swift. Use ordered containers (LinkedHashMap, slice of pairs, OrderedDictionary/array) so every SDK follows spec-declaration order.

findings.title: Unreserved/safe sets differ between SDKs: java and node in query values, and java, ruby and node in form bodies
findings.description: R8-10 aligned only the OAuth2 paths to RFC 3986 `-._~`. The regular query and form encoders were left alone. Query values (non-allowReserved): csharp, python, php, dart, go, rust, swift and elixir (and ruby, after Faraday re-encodes) keep exactly `-._~` literal. java uses `URLEncoder` plus `+`→`%20`, so `*` stays literal and `~` becomes `%7E`. node uses `encodeURIComponent`, which keeps `! * ' ( )` literal (WHATWG then turns `'` into `%27`). Form bodies: csharp, python, php, dart, go, rust, swift and elixir keep `~` and send `*` as `%2A`. java (`URLEncoder`), ruby (`URI.encode_www_form`) and node (`URLSearchParams`) keep `*` and send `~` as `%7E`. I confirmed node `k=a+b%7E*%21%27%28%29`, ruby `k=a+b%7E*%21%28%29%27` and python `k=a+b~%2A%21%28%29%27`. A compliant server decodes these the same way, but the bytes differ, which matters for signing and caching. Fix by sharing one RFC 3986 unreserved encoder per language, as the OAuth2 change did.

findings.title: Extra or missing multipart per-part headers: php adds text/plain + Content-Transfer-Encoding: 8bit, kotlin adds Content-Length, php Psr18 does not escape the field name
findings.description: php DefaultApiClient builds multipart through Symfony FormDataPart. In the bundled symfony/mime, FormDataPart::preparePart wraps every string field in `new TextPart($value, 'utf-8', 'plain', '8bit')`, and configurePart forces encoding '8bit' on every part. So every php text part carries `Content-Type: text/plain; charset=utf-8` and `Content-Transfer-Encoding: 8bit`, and file and JSON parts also carry `Content-Transfer-Encoding: 8bit`. RFC 7578 §4.7 says senders SHOULD NOT generate Content-Transfer-Encoding. The other SDKs, including php's own Psr18ApiClient, send text parts with Content-Disposition only, so php's two transports also disagree with each other. Kotlin's Ktor formData() appends a `Content-Length: N` part header to every ByteArray part (verified from the ktor-client-core 3.5.0 bytecode), which no other SDK sends. Separately, php Psr18ApiClient interpolates the field name raw into `name="…"` without backslash-escaping `"` or `\`. Every other SDK, and php's own Symfony path, escapes it.

This applies to real filenames, which come from file-handle parts: java File, go *os.File, ruby/php/python file objects, node Blob.name, swift URL, elixir {:file,…}. It is distinct from the closed 'field name as filename' item. For `résumé.pdf`:
- Most SDKs emit `filename="r_sum_.pdf"`: go, rust, node and php replace per code point; java, kotlin, csharp, dart and swift per UTF-16 unit or unicode scalar.
- python emits `filename="r?sum?.pdf"` (encode('ascii', errors='replace')).
- elixir emits `r__sum__.pdf` because it replaces per BYTE.
- ruby emits NO ASCII fallback and puts the raw UTF-8 in `filename="résumé.pdf"`, which the other SDKs deliberately avoid.
- Emoji filenames produce `__` in the UTF-16 languages and `_` in the code-point languages.
The filename* value is also encoded with different safe sets. go, php, kotlin, csharp, dart, rust, python and elixir keep only `-._~`. java (URLEncoder) and ruby (encode_www_form_component) keep `*` and encode `~`. node (encodeURIComponent) keeps `! ' ( ) *`; `'`, `(`, `)` and `*` are not RFC 5987 attr-chars, and `'` is the ext-value delimiter. swift keeps the attr-char set `!#$&+^`|`. Fix: one shared rule, using the go/php buildFilenameDirective as the canonical form. Unit test: assert the exact Content-Disposition for `résumé*(1).pdf` in each language.

findings.title: rust appends auth query params as duplicates instead of overriding an operation param of the same name
findings.description: For apiKey-in-query auth, java, kotlin, csharp, php, python, ruby, node, dart, go and swift do a map put, and elixir does Map.merge. In all of these the auth value REPLACES an operation query param with the same name. Rust's query params are a Vec and auth is `push`ed, so both `api_key=<op>&api_key=<secret>` go on the wire. It is latent: no fixture operation has a query param named like the apiKeyQuery scheme (`api_key`). Fix: in rust, replace an existing tuple with the same key.
findings.suspected_forced_reason: None

rust.note: invoke_api now drops any operation query param of the same name before pushing the authenticator's, so the name is sent once.

findings.title: A bare 'utf-16' body with a little-endian BOM decodes to garbage in csharp, swift and elixir
findings.description: java/kotlin, python, ruby, go, dart, rust, node and php honour a BOM for a bare 'utf-16' label and default to big-endian only without one. csharp returns new UnicodeEncoding(bigEndian: true, byteOrderMark: false), which does no BOM detection. swift maps it to .utf16BigEndian; I verified that FF FE 41 00 decodes to U+FFFE U+4100. elixir passes it to :unicode.characters_to_binary(:utf16), which is big-endian with no BOM handling. A LE-BOM body therefore gives a leading U+FFFE plus byte-swapped text. A BE BOM also leaves a stray U+FEFF in csharp/swift/elixir.

evidence.quote: return new UnicodeEncoding(bigEndian: true, byteOrderMark: false);

findings.suspected_forced_reason: None. Sniff FE FF / FF FE first, as go/dart/python do.
findings.note: done in csharp; still open for elixir, swift

csharp.note: csharp part only. A bare utf-16 label now sniffs a leading BOM: FF FE decodes little-endian, FE FF big-endian, and the 2-byte mark is skipped. Without a BOM it still defaults to big-endian. The swift and elixir parts belong to other agents.

findings.title: Declared-charset coverage differs: windows-1252 / shift_jis / iso-8859-x bodies decode correctly in some SDKs and as mojibake in others
findings.description: java/kotlin (all JVM charsets), csharp (with CodePagesEncodingProvider), python, ruby, php (mbstring), node (ICU TextDecoder) and rust (encoding_rs) decode any registered charset. go hard-codes utf-8/ascii/latin1/windows-1252/utf-16. swift hard-codes about 16 labels. dart supports only latin1/ascii/utf-16 and falls back to a lenient UTF-8 decode. elixir supports only latin1/utf-16/utf-32 and returns the raw bytes. So 'text/plain; charset=windows-1252' with byte 0x80 decodes to '€' in 10 SDKs but U+FFFD (dart) or invalid raw bytes (elixir). 'charset=shift_jis' also fails in go/dart/elixir.
findings.suspected_forced_reason: Partly stdlib-forced (dart/elixir have no multi-charset stdlib), but dart/elixir could at least match go's cp1252 table.

findings.title: Follow-up request headers after a 301/302 POST->GET demotion differ: go keeps Content-Type; python/rust send Content-Length: 0 on the GET
findings.description: go deletes Content-Type/Content-Length only when prevStatus == 303. net/http's header copier re-copies the ORIGINAL request's headers onto each hop, so a 301/302-demoted GET carries Content-Type: application/json with no body. python's drop_body_headers requires current_body is not None, so a body-less POST (which got the Content-Length: 0 workaround) that is 302'd to GET still sends 'Content-Length: 0'. rust deliberately keeps a literal Content-Length: 0 even when next_body is None. java/kotlin/csharp/php/ruby/node/dart/swift/elixir strip both entity headers whenever the follow-up has no body.

evidence.quote: drop_body_headers = next_body is None and current_body is not None

findings.suspected_forced_reason: None.

findings.title: Redirect-refusal error messages were never harmonized: three messages with up to six wordings each
findings.description: Several templates call these the 'harmonised cross-SDK canonical' messages, but they are not. Non-http scheme: 'Refusing to follow redirect to non-HTTP(S) URL:' (java/kotlin/python/node), '...non-http(s) URL:' (csharp/ruby/dart/rust), 'Redirect to unsupported scheme '<s>' in Location:' (php), '...non-HTTP(S) Location:' (swift), 'refusing ... non-http(s) Location (<status> redirect from a to b)' (elixir), go 'refusing to follow redirect to non-HTTP scheme "x"'. Too many: 'Too many redirects (exceeded maxRedirects) following <url>' (java), '...(exceeded maxRedirects=N)' (kotlin/php/node), '...(exceeded max_redirects=N)' (python), 'Exceeded maximum number of redirects (N)' (csharp/ruby/dart/swift), 'too many redirects (exceeded N)' (rust/elixir), go 'stopped after N redirects'. Downgrade: 12 distinct strings (e.g. java '...HTTPS->HTTP redirect: <next>', kotlin/rust '...: <cur> -> <next>', python '...HTTPS -> HTTP downgrade redirect (307) to', ruby 'Refusing to replay body across HTTPS -> HTTP redirect (TLS downgrade):'). R8-7 harmonized other messages; these were missed. Only go's lowercase is forced (ST1005).
findings.suspected_forced_reason: go must be lowercase (ST1005); the wording itself is unforced.

findings.title: Response headers drop content-encoding/content-length after decoding in rust and csharp but keep them in the other SDKs
findings.description: rust explicitly removes 'content-encoding' and 'content-length' from the returned header map after manual decompression. csharp's AutomaticDecompression strips both from Content.Headers, and swift on Apple strips Content-Encoding. java, kotlin, python, ruby, php, node, dart, go and elixir return the wire content-encoding and the compressed content-length. ApiHttpResponse.headers / ApiException.responseHeaders for the same gzip response therefore differ, and a caller comparing content-length with body length sees a mismatch only in some SDKs.
findings.suspected_forced_reason: csharp/swift are runtime-driven, so the remaining 9 could match by stripping, or rust could stop stripping.

rust.note: The stripping is deliberate: default_api_client.mustache around line 443 comments that the headers describe the decoded body, as when reqwest decompressed it. csharp and swift strip because of their runtimes. Which side moves is a cross-SDK ruling, and no template change was made.

findings.title: csharp alone enables online certificate-revocation checking
findings.description: HttpClientHandler is built with CheckCertificateRevocationList = true. With verifySsl=true and no caCertPath, .NET fetches CRL/OCSP on every new TLS connection. If the revocation endpoint is unreachable (air-gapped/egress-restricted hosts), chain building reports RevocationStatusUnknown and the handshake fails, while the same endpoint works in the other 11, none of which check revocation. The caCertPath branch sets RevocationMode.NoCheck, so behaviour also differs within csharp.
findings.suspected_forced_reason: None (it may be there for an analyzer rule such as CA5400, which can be suppressed with a rationale).

findings.title: dart AbstractApiClient drops a Map (multipart) body on a 307/308 replay (latent: BaseApi pre-serializes)
findings.description: sendRequest accepts a Map<String, Object?> body and builds an http.MultipartRequest for the first hop. The redirect loop rebuilds only Uint8List and String bodies, so a 307/308 replays the method with an empty body (and the stale Content-Type). Generated operations are safe because dart BaseApi serializes multipart to Uint8List first, but the public ApiClient.sendRequest contract still loses data. The comment claims String handling fixed the multipart replay.
findings.suspected_forced_reason: None. Serialize the Map to bytes once before the first send.

dart.note: Confirmed. The redirect loop now rebuilds a Map body with _buildMultipartRequest on 307/308, finalizes it to bytes and sets the new boundary's Content-Type. A stale Content-Type without a boundary is overridden.
dart.test: default_api_client_unit_test.mustache: 'a Map multipart body is replayed intact across a 307 redirect'

findings.title: kotlin treats every 300-399 status as a redirect; the other 11 follow only 301/302/303/307/308
findings.description: kotlin's loop condition is response.status.value in 300..399, so a 300 Multiple Choices (or 305/306) carrying a Location is followed, as a GET demotion for non-GET. Its exhaustion check uses the same range. java isRedirect, csharp/php/python/ruby/node/dart/rust/elixir redirect_status? and go/swift (platform) use only 301/302/303/307/308, so a 300+Location surfaces as a 300 error everywhere except kotlin.
findings.suspected_forced_reason: None.

kotlin.note: Real. Added isRedirectStatus (301/302/303/307/308) and used it in both the follow loop and the exhaustion check. A 300 or 305 with a Location is now returned as-is.
kotlin.test: DefaultApiClientUnitTest.kt: '300 and 305 with a Location are returned as-is, never followed' and 'only 301, 302, 303, 307 and 308 are redirect statuses'

findings.title: Named status errors do not always pin their status: the csharp (message, inner) constructor gives StatusCode 0, and dart, swift and rust accept any status
findings.description: In java, kotlin, php, python, ruby, node and elixir, each leaf (BadRequest through InternalServerError) hard-codes its status, for example java `super(400, …)` and elixir `status_code: 400`. (go leaves cannot be constructed outside FromResponse.) The exceptions are as follows. In csharp, every leaf's (string message, Exception innerException) constructor chains to ApiException(message, inner), which never sets StatusCode, so `new NotFoundException("x", inner).StatusCode == 0`. In dart, every leaf takes `required super.statusCode`, so `BadRequestException(statusCode: 500, …)` is legal. swift leaves are empty subclasses that inherit ApiError.init(statusCode:…), defaulting to 0. In rust, BadRequestError::from(ClientError) accepts any inner status. A NotFoundError reporting status 0 or 500 breaks the type/status invariant the factory guarantees.

evidence.quote:
public BadRequestException(string message, Exception innerException)
        : base(message, innerException) { }

findings.note: done in csharp; still open for dart, rust, swift

csharp.note: csharp part only. Added (int statusCode, string message, Exception inner) constructors to ClientException and ServerException, and each leaf (400, 401, 403, 404, 409, 422, 500) chains its (message, inner) constructor to them, so StatusCode is pinned. The dart, swift and rust parts belong to other agents.

findings.title: OAuth2TokenError messages and cause retention were never harmonised across the 12
findings.description: The canonical strings, used by java, csharp, python, ruby, node and dart, are 'Token response is not valid JSON: <detail>' for an unparseable 2xx body, 'Token response is not a JSON object' for valid non-object JSON, and 'Token response missing or empty access_token field'. The outliers are: rust 'failed to parse token response: <e>' and a lowercase 'token response missing or empty access_token field', with a JSON array body (`[]`) reported as the missing-access_token message; swift and elixir 'Token response is not a valid token JSON object' for both the invalid-JSON and non-object cases; kotlin 'Token response is not a JSON object: <detail>' for invalid JSON; php 'Token response is not a JSON object' for invalid JSON (json_decode returns null); go reports a non-object body as 'Token response is not valid JSON: json: cannot unmarshal array…'. Cause retention also differs. java, kotlin, csharp and python (and ruby's implicit cause) keep the parser exception. The node, dart, go, rust and elixir OAuth2TokenError types and the swift enum have no cause slot at all, and php does not pass $previous. R8-7 harmonised the sibling OIDC/bearer messages but not these.

evidence.quote: throw OAuth2TokenError.invalidResponse("Token response is not a valid token JSON object")
message: "Token response is not a valid token JSON object"
throw OAuth2TokenException("Token response is not a JSON object: ${e.message}", e)
throw new OAuth2TokenException("Token response is not valid JSON: " + e.getMessage(), e);

findings.title: The 'Response headers:' line of the rendered error uses 12 different map syntaxes, and java's order is nondeterministic
findings.description: The rendered error string otherwise uses identical labels, but the headers value is each language's native map dump: java/kotlin/csharp `{k=v}`, php/node JSON `{"k":"v"}`, python `{'k': 'v'}`, ruby `{"k" => "v"}`, dart `{k: v}`, go `map[k:v]`, rust Debug `{"k": "v"}`, swift `["k": "v"]`, elixir `%{"k" => "v"}`. Log scrapers and the cross-SDK rendering tests therefore cannot share one expected string. java is also non-deterministic. The constructor stores Map.copyOf(responseHeaders), whose ImmutableCollections.MapN iteration order is salted per JVM run, so the same error renders headers in a different order from run to run. kotlin's toMap() and csharp's Dictionary preserve order. A canonical `k: v` join, or JSON in insertion order, would make this uniform.

findings.title: fromResponse error-body parsing skips the BOM strip that the success path applies (BOM-prefixed body: only java and swift populate errorBody)
findings.description: Every success-path deserializer except node's strips a leading U+FEFF (each carries the 'RFC 8259 §8.1 … Windows-generated payloads' comment). The error-body parse in fromResponse mostly does not. java goes through ObjectSerializer.deserialize, which strips. swift's JSONSerialization tolerates a BOM (confirmed by script). kotlin parseToJsonElement, csharp JsonDocument.Parse (its own ObjectSerializer comment says System.Text.Json throws on a string BOM), php json_decode, python/ruby/node/dart parse_json, go unmarshalErrorBody, rust serde_json::from_str and elixir parse_json are all called raw, so they leave errorBody null. I confirmed with scripts that python json.loads, node JSON.parse and ruby JSON.parse each reject a BOM. node has no BOM strip anywhere, so its success-path deserialize also rejects a BOM payload that the other 11 accept. Fix: strip the BOM inside each parse_json/parseJson helper, which both paths share.

findings.title: kotlin and go parse the OAuth2 §5.2 error object differently from the other 10 (non-string fields)
findings.description: java, csharp, php, python, ruby, node, dart, rust, swift and elixir require `error` to be a non-empty JSON string, and type-check error_description and error_uri independently, setting a non-string value to null. kotlin uses `root["error"]?.jsonPrimitive?.contentOrNull`, which coerces a numeric or boolean `error` (`{"error":400}`) into the code "400", where the others report code=null and the raw-body message. The same class of coercion was fixed for refresh_token in T2-12. kotlin also calls .jsonPrimitive on description and uri: a non-primitive description throws, the catch-all fires, and the whole parse falls back to code=null and the raw body. go decodes into a struct with string fields, so any non-string description or uri makes json.Unmarshal fail and also discards a valid code. Example: `{"error":"invalid_grant","error_description":{"en":"x"}}` gives the message '…: invalid_grant' in 10 SDKs and '…: {raw body}' with code=null in kotlin and go. go additionally treats an empty description "" as absent, so the message omits ' -- ', where the others render '… -- '. This is forced only to the extent that go's getters return string, not *string.

kotlin.note: Kotlin part only. A new jsonStringOrNull helper requires a JSON string for error, error_description and error_uri. A numeric error no longer becomes code '400'. A non-string description or uri is dropped independently and the valid code is kept. The go part was not touched.

go.note: Same root cause as F114 and fixed by the same change on the go side. The empty-description difference (go renders no ' -- ' for '') is left as is: go's getters return string, which AGENTS.md notes as forced, and the code cannot tell absent from empty without a field change. Kotlin half untouched.

findings.title: python, ruby and elixir render an empty detail message as empty instead of the default text
findings.description: java, kotlin, csharp, php, node, dart, go, rust and swift substitute 'Error message: the server returns an error' when the detail message is null OR empty (isEmpty, === '', == ""). python (`if self.message is None`), ruby (`@message.nil?`) and elixir (`error.message || …`, where "" is truthy) substitute it only for nil. An error built with message "" therefore renders an empty first line in those three. This is reachable when wrapping a transport exception whose own message is empty, for example str(e) == ''.

evidence.quote: msg = @message.nil? ? 'Error message: the server returns an error' : @message
msg = error.message || "Error message: the server returns an error"

ruby.test: test/api_error_test.mustache: 'substitutes the default text for an empty detail message'

python.note: ApiException.__str__ now uses 'self.message or default', so an empty message renders the default text like None does. Ruby and elixir are other agents' files.

elixir.note: ApiError.message/1 now treats "" like nil and substitutes 'Error message: the server returns an error'. This is the elixir part only; the python and ruby parts are not mine.
elixir.test: test/api_error_test.mustache: 'an empty message renders the default text, like a missing one'

findings.title: ruby has no accessor for the bare detail message: #message returns the full multi-line rendering
findings.description: Eleven SDKs keep the detail message ('API returned status code 404') separate from the rendered string: java/kotlin getMessage, csharp Message, php getMessage, python .message, node .message, dart .message, go Msg(), rust message(), swift .message, and the elixir struct's :message field (Exception.message/1 renders). java's template comment says this holds for 'all twelve SDKs'. ruby overrides #message to return the rendering, and to_s delegates to it. The constructor's detail string lives only in the @message ivar, which has no reader, so a ruby caller cannot get the detail message the other 11 expose. The nearest documented forcing feature is Ruby's Exception#message -> to_s, which would be satisfied by keeping message/to_s rendered and adding a `detail_message` reader. Nothing forces having no detail accessor at all. The java comment is false for ruby.

evidence.quote: caller reads, and all twelve SDKs render the response context through

findings.title: rust's per-status error wrappers render a different, context-free string from ApiError and from the other SDKs
findings.description: ApiError::from_response returns a Box holding BadRequestError, NotFoundError, ClientError and so on. Each wrapper has its own Display, for example 'Not found (404): API returned status code 404', 'Client error (418): …' or 'Network error: …'. These drop the 'HTTP status code' / 'Response headers' / 'Response body' lines that ApiError's Display (and every other SDK's string form for the same typed error) renders. ApiErrorKind adds a third format, 'API error (status N): …'. So err.to_string() for a 404 from any rust operation differs from java toString, python str, go Error() and the rest, and loses the response body in logs. Fix: have each wrapper's Display delegate to the inner ApiError's Display.

findings.title: swift OAuth2TokenError does not conform to LocalizedError: localizedDescription is the generic Foundation text
findings.description: Every other swift SDK error conforms to LocalizedError (ApiError, SerializationError, OAuth2ServerError and ConfigurationError), and every other language's OAuth2TokenError renders its message. swift's OAuth2TokenError is a bare enum (missingAccessToken(String) / invalidResponse(String)) with no errorDescription and no message accessor. I confirmed with a swift script that error.localizedDescription is "The operation couldn’t be completed. (….OAuth2TokenError error 0.)" and that the message text never appears. Its shape (two cases) also differs from the single-message type in the other 11. Minimal fix: add `extension OAuth2TokenError: LocalizedError` that returns the associated string.

swift.note: Added extension OAuth2TokenError: LocalizedError returning the associated message for both cases.

findings.title: 'Whitespace-only' detection uses each language's native trim, so the 12 SDKs accept and reject different API-key values
findings.description: Every SDK rejects an empty or whitespace-only key or token, but each uses its own stdlib whitespace set: java Character.isWhitespace, kotlin isBlank, .NET IsNullOrWhiteSpace, php trim (" \t\n\r\0\x0B", which includes NUL and not \f), python str.strip, ruby strip (ASCII plus NUL), JS trim, go TrimSpace, dart trim, rust trim, swift .whitespacesAndNewlines, elixir String.trim. I checked java, kotlin-on-JVM, python, ruby, node, rust and swift locally. For a QUERY or COOKIE API key, where non-ASCII is allowed, the results are: "\f" is accepted only by php (sent as the credential); "\x1f" is rejected as empty by java, kotlin and python and accepted by the other 9; U+00A0 is accepted by java, php and ruby (elixir probably too) and rejected by kotlin, csharp, python, node, go, dart, rust and swift; U+0085 is accepted by java, kotlin, php, ruby and node and rejected by the rest; "\0" gives 'must not be empty' in php and ruby but 'contains forbidden control characters' elsewhere. For Bearer the input is always rejected but the message differs, e.g. "\f" gives 'printable ASCII' in java and php and 'must not be empty' elsewhere. Fix: define one whitespace set, e.g. ASCII SP/HTAB/CR/LF/VT/FF or the Unicode White_Space property, and implement it explicitly per language instead of calling the native trim. Add a shared table test.

findings.title: In all 12 SDKs, a token that is only the 'Bearer ' prefix passes the empty-token guard and sends a credential-less Authorization header
findings.description: The constructors reject an empty or whitespace-only token so that 'Authorization: Bearer ' is never sent. Prefix de-duplication runs later, in getAuthHeaders, so the token "Bearer " (or "bearer    ") is not whitespace-only and passes construction. Stripping the 7-char prefix then emits `Authorization: Bearer ` or `Authorization: Bearer    `, the exact unauthenticated request the guard exists to prevent. The behaviour is the same in all 12 (so not a parity gap), but the guard is ineffective in every SDK. The likely real-world case is an env var templated as `Bearer ${TOKEN}` with TOKEN unset. Fix: in every constructor, strip the prefix first and then apply the empty and ASCII checks. Unit test: `BearerAuthenticator(host, "Bearer ")` must raise 'Bearer token must not be empty'.

findings.title: PARITY_TODO T2-8 is still listed as open/DEFERRED, but rust now declares the per-scheme authenticator modules
findings.description: PARITY_TODO T2-8 says rust `auth/mod.rs` omits the 8 scheme-authenticator `mod` declarations and leaves the item unchecked as deferred. The golden `rust/src/auth/mod.rs` now has `pub mod pet_store_basic_authenticator; ... pub mod session_cookie_authenticator;`, and `auth/oauth/mod.rs` declares the OAuth wrappers. AGENTS.md (the needsApiKeyLocation note) says these modules surfaced once T2-8 declared them. The TODO item is stale and should be checked off with a pointer to the AGENTS note.

findings.title: Per-scheme wrapper authenticators print differently across languages: java falls back to Object.toString, rust has no Debug, node/go/elixir print the base class name
findings.description: AGENTS records authenticator debug field-sets as uniform, but the generated per-scheme wrappers (SessionCookieAuthenticator, AdminBasicAuthenticator, ...) break this. java wraps by composition (forced by `final` bases and SpotBugs CT_CONSTRUCTOR_THROW, as the template says) but never delegates `toString()`. `new SessionCookieAuthenticator(h,k).toString()` therefore gives `com.example.petstore.auth.SessionCookieAuthenticator@1b6d3586`, with no host, keyParamName or location. kotlin, csharp, python, ruby, dart, swift and php show `SessionCookieAuthenticator(host=..., keyParamName=SESSION_ID, apiKey=***, location=COOKIE)`. The rust newtype `pub struct X(ApiKeyAuthenticator)` has no Debug impl, so `{:?}` does not compile and any user struct that derives Debug cannot hold a wrapper. node's inspect hook hard-codes `ApiKeyAuthenticator(` / `BearerAuthenticator(` instead of `this.constructor.name`, so wrappers print as the base class. go (embedding) and elixir (whose `new/2` returns the base struct) also show the base name. Secrets stay masked; only the non-secret field-set and type name drift. Fix: java wrapper template should override toString using the delegate's fields and the wrapper's simple name; rust should add a Debug impl that delegates; node should use `this.constructor.name`.

findings.title: The apiKey scheme name is pasted into each language's string literal without escaping, so legal header names can break or silently change some SDKs
findings.description: Each Better<Lang>Codegen builds the wrapper's super-call by concatenating `spec.keyParamName()` inside a hard-coded quote character, with HTML escaping disabled: single quotes in php, node, ruby and dart; double quotes in java, kotlin, csharp, python, go, rust, swift and elixir. RFC 7230 tchar allows `'`, `$` and backquote in header and cookie names, and OpenAPI query names may contain anything. So: a header named `X-Api'Key` gives a syntax error in php, node, ruby and dart but compiles in the other 8. A name containing `$ident` becomes Dart or Kotlin string interpolation; `$apiKey` would even splice the secret into the header name. A query name containing `"` or `\` breaks the double-quote languages. The same unescaped value feeds the redirect strip-list templates. Fix: escape per target language (one helper per codegen). Extend the probe spec with an apiKey scheme whose name contains `'` and `$` so the build and lint specs exercise it.

findings.title: elixir omits secret fields from inspect output instead of showing '***' as the other 11 do
findings.description: elixir uses `@derive {Inspect, except: [:token]}` (likewise :api_key and :password). The secret field therefore disappears from `inspect/1` output rather than appearing as a masked field. The other 11 render it as `token=***` / `apiKey: ***` / `'password' => '***'`, and their tests assert the `***` marker, which elixir's tests cannot. Secrets do not leak. Note that `inspect(auth, structs: false)` bypasses the Inspect protocol entirely and prints the raw map with the secret. A hand-written `defimpl Inspect` that emits `token: "***"` would match the other 11 and close the `structs: false` hole.

elixir.note: Replaced @derive {Inspect, except: ...} with a defimpl Inspect that masks the secret fields as "***" (nil stays nil) in all 8 authenticators: bearer, api_key, basic, implicit, auth_code, client_credentials, password and OIDC. The finding's claim that this closes the inspect(structs: false) hole is wrong, because that option bypasses the Inspect protocol entirely, so that hole remains.
elixir.test: The existing redaction tests in test/bearer_authenticator_test, api_key_authenticator_test, basic_authenticator_test, oauth2_auth_code_authenticator_test, oauth2_client_credentials_authenticator_test, oauth2_password_authenticator_test, oauth2_implicit_authenticator_test and openid_connect_authenticator_test (.mustache) now also assert the masked field, e.g. token: "***"

findings.title: go and rust auth error texts differ from the canonical strings in ways ST1005 does not require (contradicts the R8-7 'harmonised' claim)
findings.description: Canonical texts are `API key value for 'X' must not be empty`, `Bearer token must not be empty` and `Basic auth username must not contain ...`. go wraps sentinels so the canonical phrase changes shape: `invalid API key: value for 'X' must not be empty` and `invalid bearer token: token must not be empty`. ST1005 only forbids a capitalised first word. It accepts a leading initialism such as 'API', and it would allow `bearer token must not be empty`. go's own required-parameter sentinel ('missing the required parameter ...') shows the sentinel can keep the canonical wording. go's Basic messages are canonical apart from forced lowercase. rust's BasicAuthenticator adds an extra rust-only prefix inside InvalidArgument: `invalid HTTP Basic credentials: Basic auth username must not contain ':' ...`. rust's ApiKey/Bearer and swift's Basic do not have it, and the rust test locks it in. The go bearer test asserts only the suffix 'token must not be empty', so the drift went unnoticed. Fix: use canonical (lowercased-only-where-forced) phrasing after the sentinel, and drop the rust Basic prefix.

fmt.Errorf("%w: value for '%s' must not be empty", ErrInvalidApiKey, keyParamName)

findings.title: python (and the node test) have a template comment that renders as '(X-API-Key, X-Internal-Key, )' with a dangling separator
findings.description: The python default_api_client template and the node unit-test template iterate `apiKeyHeaderNames` with an unconditional `{{name}}, ` and no `{{^-last}}` guard. The generated comment reads `The spec-declared API-key header names (X-API-Key, X-Internal-Key, )`. This is cosmetic only, and the other templates guard the separator with `-last`.

evidence.quote: # The spec-declared API-key header names (X-API-Key, X-Internal-Key, )

findings.title: python authenticators compare and hash by value, including the secret; every other SDK except elixir and php's loose == uses identity
findings.description: ApiKey/Basic/Bearer (and the OAuth ones) are `@dataclass(frozen=True)` with the default `eq=True`. Two separately built authenticators with the same host and secret are therefore `==`, and they hash equal, which makes them usable as set or dict keys by value. Equality also compares the secret. java, kotlin, csharp, swift, dart, node, ruby and go (pointers) use reference identity, and rust implements no PartialEq. elixir structs (BEAM, forced) and php `==` (language, forced) are structural. python can turn value equality off with `@dataclass(frozen=True, eq=False)`, so its difference is not forced. Decide on identity (the majority) and add a test that two equal-credential authenticators are not `==`.

python.note: All five authenticator dataclasses (ApiKey, Basic, Bearer, OAuth2 client-credentials, OAuth2 password) are now @dataclass(frozen=True, eq=False), so they compare and hash by identity. The secret is no longer compared or hashed by value.
python.test: test_api_key_authenticator.py, test_basic_authenticator.py, test_bearer_authenticator.py, test_oauth2_client_credentials_authenticator.py and test_oauth2_password_authenticator.py, each: test_equal_credentials_are_not_equal_by_value

findings.title: ruby per-scheme wrappers take keyword arguments while their base authenticators (and every other SDK's wrappers) take positional ones
findings.description: `SessionCookieAuthenticator.new(host:, api_key:)`, `AdminBasicAuthenticator.new(host:, username:, password:)` and `ServiceTokenAuthenticator.new(host:, token:)` are keyword-only. The bases they subclass are positional (`ApiKeyAuthenticator.new(host, key_param_name, api_key, location)`, `BearerAuthenticator.new(host, token)`). So `ServiceTokenAuthenticator.new('h','t')` raises ArgumentError, while the matching base call works. In java, kotlin, csharp, php, python, node, go, rust, swift and elixir the wrappers are positional like their bases. dart is named everywhere, which is consistent within dart. The RBS sig matches the code, so steep does not catch the mismatch, and no test constructs a ruby wrapper. Fix: pick one convention for ruby and use it for both base and wrapper.

findings.title: rust appends authenticator query params instead of overriding, so a same-named query parameter is sent twice
findings.description: The other 11 SDKs merge `getQueryParams()` into a map keyed by name (java put, python update, go map assign, dart addAll, elixir Map.merge, ...), so the authenticator's api_key replaces any same-named operation query parameter and the URL carries exactly one `api_key=`. rust keeps a Vec of tuples and `push`es the authenticator's entries, so the URL carries both `api_key=<user>&api_key=<secret>`, and which value wins depends on the server. This is latent: no petstore operation has a query parameter named after the apiKeyQuery scheme (`api_key`). To pin it, add a petstore or probe operation secured by apiKeyQuery that also declares an optional `in: query, name: api_key` parameter, and assert a single occurrence. Fix: remove any existing entry with the same key before pushing.

rust.note: Same defect as F256, fixed by the same change.

findings.title: AGENTS R8-9 contradicted: OAuth authenticator redacted-repr field sets are still not unified
findings.description: R8-9/AGENTS say the non-secret field sets of the OAuth2 reprs were unified across all 12, but the code disagrees. Auth-code: java/kotlin/rust show 8 fields; python/go/csharp omit refreshUrl; php/swift/dart/elixir add tokenExchanged; node and ruby show only host, clientId and clientSecret. OIDC: java/kotlin/rust/php/python/swift/dart show 6; go omits scopes; ruby and csharp show 4; node shows 3; elixir's derived Inspect also dumps api_client, discovery_expiry and discovery_cache. go's ClientAuthMethod has no String(), so CC/password reprs print 0/1 instead of BODY/BASIC (the same class of issue R8 fixed for ApiKeyLocation). node hardcodes the base class name in inspect output, while the other languages print the runtime subclass name.

findings.title: Auth-code precondition messages drift (kotlin 'or blank', ruby lowercase, rust/go prefixed wording, swift has no message)
findings.description: Canonical (java/csharp/php/python/node/dart/elixir): 'Authorization code must not be empty' and 'Must call exchangeCode() before making API requests' (idiomatic method name). kotlin: 'Authorization code must not be empty or blank'. ruby: lowercase 'authorization code must not be empty'. rust: 'oauth2 authorization code: code must not be empty' and '…: must call exchange_code before requesting auth headers' (rust is not lowercase-forced; R8-7 moved its other messages to canonical capitalized forms). swift: OAuth2AuthorizationCodeError.emptyCode/.codeNotExchanged has no description/LocalizedError, so the message is the generic Foundation text, unlike swift's implicit flow which uses ConfigurationError with the canonical text. go is lowercase per ST1005 but its wording also differs from the canonical sentence.

findings.title: Constructor shape drift: refreshUrl position and python's silent defaults for required OAuth config
findings.description: java (password and auth-code), kotlin (password only) and csharp put refreshUrl right after tokenUrl, before username/redirectUri. kotlin's auth-code constructor and php/python/ruby/node/dart/go/rust/swift/elixir put it last as an optional. Kotlin is even inconsistent between its own two flows. python's frozen dataclasses default token_url="", username="", password="" (and scopes=()), so OAuth2PasswordAuthenticator(host, id, secret) constructs fine and only fails at the first request by POSTing to "". In every other language these are required arguments. Not forced: a dataclass field without a default may follow client_secret.

findings.title: Generator emits OAuth scopes in HashMap order, not spec order
findings.description: SchemeAuthSpec copies flow.getScopes() (a LinkedHashMap from swagger-parser) into `new HashMap<>(scopes)`, so the wrappers emit ["pets:write","pets:read"] although the spec declares pets:read first. The order is deterministic only by accident of hash buckets, and it changes the scope= string on the wire. Use LinkedHashMap.

evidence.quote: this.scopes = scopes != null ? Collections.unmodifiableMap(new HashMap<>(scopes)) : null;

findings.title: Non-JSON 2xx token body echoed into OAuth2TokenError message (ruby, kotlin; node/java partially) — can leak the access/refresh token into logs
findings.description: Redaction parity. When the 2xx token body is not JSON (e.g. a form-encoded 'access_token=gho_…&token_type=bearer' answer, or a truncated JSON), ruby's message includes JSON::ParserError#message, which quotes the whole input (probed: "unexpected token at 'access_token=gho_SECRET123&token_type=bearer'"); kotlinx-serialization exceptions append a 'JSON input: …' excerpt; node's V8 SyntaxError quotes the first ~10 characters; Jackson 2.19 quotes the unrecognized token text. python/csharp/go/rust/dart/swift/elixir/php messages carry no body content. The SDKs carefully redact secrets in reprs; the token error path should not echo the body either.

evidence.quote: raise ...OAuth2TokenError, "Token response is not valid JSON: #{e.message}"

findings.title: Sync auth-header accessor on token-based OAuth flows: csharp throws, node/dart (and go/rust's infallible variants) silently return {}
findings.description: Among the value-wrapped-async SDKs, csharp's GetAuthHeaders() on the CC/password/auth-code/OIDC authenticators throws InvalidOperationException ('use GetAuthHeadersAsync() instead'). node getAuthHeaders() and dart authHeaders() return an empty map, and dart's auth-code authenticator returns {} even after exchange. go AuthHeaders() and rust auth_headers() also swallow errors into {}; go's auth-code variant logs while its CC variant does not. A caller using the sync/infallible accessor gets fail-loud behaviour in one SDK and a silently unauthenticated request in the others. AGENTS documents the method shape, not this behaviour.

findings.title: Test-coverage gaps: refresh-failure fallback (2/12), OIDC max-age and rediscovery (0/12), wrapper scopes (0/12)
findings.description: Only csharp (RefreshFailureWithMalformedBodyFallsBackToOriginalGrant) and php ('rejected refresh token falls back to the original grant') test the refresh-fails-then-re-run-the-original-grant path. The other 10 token-manager suites have no such test. No language tests Cache-Control max-age parsing, rediscovery, or token state surviving rediscovery. No language asserts the per-scheme wrappers send the spec scopes. These gaps hide the high-severity findings above. All of these are unit-testable against the existing petstore schemes; no spec expansion is needed.

findings.title: Token-request body and authorize-URL parameter order differ (java hash order, go/elixir sorted, rust/swift random per process)
findings.description: Same input, different bytes. kotlin/csharp/php/python/ruby/node/dart emit insertion order (grant_type, client_id, client_secret, scope). java builds params in HashMap and iterates hash order: grant_type, scope, client_secret, client_id (computed). go url.Values.Encode() and elixir URI.encode_query(map) sort keys (client_id, client_secret, grant_type, scope; authorize URL client_id, redirect_uri, response_type, scope, state). rust (HashMap with RandomState) and swift (Dictionary with per-process seeded hashing) change the order between runs, so their token bodies are non-deterministic. Semantically equivalent for a form decoder, but it violates the byte-identical rule and makes byte-level golden assertions impossible. Use insertion-ordered containers (LinkedHashMap, ordered slice, Vec, KeyValuePairs, keyword list).

findings.title: buildAuthorizationUrl with an empty state: 6 SDKs emit '&state=', 6 omit it
findings.description: For both the auth-code and implicit builders, state="" is appended as '&state=' by java/kotlin/csharp/php (null checks) and ruby/elixir ("" is truthy), but dropped by python/node (falsy), go/rust/swift/dart (empty-string sentinel). Pick one rule; treating "" as absent matches the languages that cannot express null.

findings.title: expires_in string grammar differs (hex, type suffixes, newline trimming)
findings.description: Quoted expires_in values are parsed with each runtime's own number grammar. For "0x10", ruby Float(), JS Number() and swift Double() return 16 while the other languages give 0 (stale). java's Double.parseDouble accepts "3600d"/"3600f" (probed: 3600). swift trims only .whitespaces, so "3600\n" becomes 0 where every other SDK gets 3600. Use one decimal-digits(+fraction) grammar in all 12.

findings.title: An unreadable caCertPath with verifySsl=false is rejected by 7 SDKs and accepted by 5
findings.description: java, kotlin, csharp, php and python check the CA only in the `else if (caCertPath != null)` branch after `!verifySsl`, so with verifySsl=false a missing or garbage CA path is ignored. ruby, node, elixir and swift validate at construction regardless of verifySsl, dart calls setTrustedCertificates before checking verifySsl, and go/rust read the file in TransportOptions build(). Those 7 throw a configuration error for the same input. A shared rule is needed (validate whenever the field is set, or never when verification is off).

findings.title: PARITY_TODO R8-F3 says only dart and swift treat an empty proxy as 'no proxy'; go and rust do too
findings.description: R8-F3 lists 'dart/swift empty-string-proxy leniency' as the documented residual. go's Proxy("") and rust's proxy("") also return early with no proxy and no error. Both take a non-optional string, so "" is their only way to clear it. java, kotlin, csharp, php, python, ruby, node and elixir reject "" as an invalid proxy URL. The note should list all four.

findings.title: Proxy validation messages differ per failure, and swift drops the reason entirely
findings.description: Canonical forms used by most SDKs: 'Invalid proxy URL: X', 'Invalid proxy URL (must use http or https scheme): X', 'Invalid proxy URL (missing host): X'. Divergences: swift throws invalidProxyURL(val) for all three causes, so the message is always 'Invalid proxy URL: X' with no reason. node's unparseable case says 'Invalid proxy URL (unparseable): X'. ruby embeds the URI library message, e.g. 'Invalid proxy URL (bad URI(is not URI?): ...): X'. kotlin reports a missing '://' as '(missing scheme)'. rust renders `invalid proxy URL: "X": must use http or https scheme`, lower-case with a Debug-quoted value; only go's lower-case is ST1005-forced. CA-file messages likewise vary ('failed to read or parse', 'failed to load', 'failed to read'/'failed to parse', Invalid CA certificate: ...).

findings.title: Server-variable error message renders the allowed-values list 5 different ways, contradicting R8-7
findings.description: PARITY_TODO R8-7 says the server-variable message (T3-17) was harmonised to one canonical string. The prefix is shared, but the list is formatted by each language's default collection rendering. Same input, 5 renderings: `[api, staging, sandbox]` (java, kotlin, csharp, dart); `api, staging, sandbox` (php, node); `['api', 'staging', 'sandbox']` (python repr); `["api", "staging", "sandbox"]` (ruby, swift, rust, elixir inspect/Debug); `[api staging sandbox]` (go %v). rust also double-prefixes via Display: `invalid server variable: Invalid value ...`. go's lower-case `invalid value` is ST1005-forced; the list format is not. No test in any language asserts the full message (java/python/node/php assert only the type, kotlin/csharp/ruby a substring), which is how this survived.

evidence.quote: "%w: invalid value '%s' for server variable '%s'. Allowed values: %v"
"Invalid value '{}' for server variable '{}'. Allowed values: {:?}"
server-variable (T3-17) ... all harmonized to one canonical string per message

findings.title: The 'not already set' checks for User-Agent and X-Request-ID are case-sensitive in all 12, so the wire result varies by HTTP library
findings.description: Every client merges transport defaults and request headers into a case-sensitive map, then checks the exact strings `User-Agent` and `X-Request-ID` before injecting (java/kotlin/python containsKey/`in`, csharp a default-comparer Dictionary, php isset, ruby `||=`, node a property lookup, go/swift/elixir map keys, dart containsKey). A caller who sets `user-agent` or `x-request-id` in lower case through Configuration.defaultHeader or TransportOptions.defaultHeader gets a second, injected header. What reaches the wire then depends on the library (inferred from library semantics, not run here): java/python send two header lines; node's Headers joins them into `MyApp, petstore-client/1.0.0 (node)`; go (http.Header canonicalisation), rust (HeaderMap) and swift (URLRequest.setValue) keep whichever was written last, which follows randomised map iteration order and so is non-deterministic. The caller's override should win in all 12, so the lookup should be case-insensitive.

findings.title: The default User-Agent product token comes from a different identifier in different SDKs
findings.description: Each Better<Lang>Codegen builds userAgentDefault differently. java/kotlin use invokerPackage (`com.example.petstore/1.0.0 (java)`), not the spec-derived Maven artifactId `petstore-client` that R?-T3-7 introduced for parity. php uses the PHP namespace (`PetstoreClient`), not the composer package. python uses the import name `petstore_client`, not the distribution `petstore-client`. node uses npmName (`petstore-client`), ruby gemName, and csharp/dart/elixir/rust/swift/go their packageName. The token goes on the wire with every request, so server-side analytics see unrelated names for the same SDK family. Pick one source (the published package name) for all 12.

findings.title: java puts TraceContextUtil in the api subpackage; the other 11 keep it at the SDK root
findings.description: java generates com.example.petstore.api.TraceContextUtil (and the test lives in .../api/). kotlin, csharp and the rest place it next to Configuration and TransportOptions in the root package/namespace. No Java rule forces this: BaseApi could import it from the root package.

findings.title: kotlin and php reject an upper-case proxy scheme (HTTP://...) that the other 10 accept
findings.description: kotlin hand-parses the scheme and checks `scheme !in listOf("http", "https")` case-sensitively. php compares parse_url()['scheme'], which keeps the original case, with !== 'http'. Both throw 'Invalid proxy URL (must use http or https scheme)' for HTTP://proxy:3128. The other 10 accept it: java uses equalsIgnoreCase, csharp/python/node/dart/go/rust/elixir parsers lowercase the scheme (python/node/ruby verified locally), ruby downcases, and swift lowercases. RFC 3986 schemes are case-insensitive. kotlin's ad-hoc parser also differs elsewhere: a string with no '://' gets a distinct '(missing scheme)' message, and `http://@:3128` passes its host check while java's URI-based check rejects it. Ktor's common io.ktor.http.Url is available, so the hand parser is not forced.
findings.note: done in php; still open for kotlin

php.test: tests/TransportOptionsTest.php: 'proxy scheme is matched case insensitively'

findings.title: node per-operation variants replace only the first {var}; node and ruby also expand $&/\0 patterns in server-variable values
findings.description: node's per-operation server variants substitute with `url.replace("{" + name + "}", value)`, which replaces only the first occurrence. The other 11 replace every occurrence (java/kotlin String.replace, csharp Replace, go ReplaceAll, python str.replace, php str_replace, ruby gsub, dart replaceAll, rust replace, swift replacingOccurrences, elixir String.replace), as does node's own global ServerConfiguration.getUrl (replaceAll). A template that uses a variable twice keeps a literal `{var}` in node only. Separately, node's String.replace/replaceAll and ruby's gsub treat the replacement as a pattern: `$&`, `$$`, `` $` `` in JS and `\0`, `\&`, `\\` in ruby are expanded. A free-form (non-enum) server variable such as `a$&b` (node) or `a\0b` (ruby) is mangled, giving `a{v}b` (verified locally), while the other 10 substitute literally.
findings.note: done in node; still open for ruby

findings.title: php, python, node and ruby let callers skip proxy validation through a public TransportOptions constructor
findings.description: Proxy validation lives only in the builder's proxy() method. java (package-private ctor), kotlin (private), csharp (internal; PARITY_TODO T2-10 says TransportOptions is builder-only 'because it has validated invariants'), dart (TransportOptions._), swift (fileprivate init), go (unexported fields) and rust (private fields) make the builder the only way in, and elixir validates inside new/1. php's TransportOptions::__construct is public with defaults, python's frozen dataclass has a public __init__ and __post_init__ only freezes headers, node's constructor is public, and ruby's initialize is public. In those four, `new TransportOptions(proxy: 'ftp://x')` or `TransportOptions(proxy='ftp://x')` is accepted and the bad value only fails later inside the HTTP library, where it can be misclassified as a NetworkError instead of a caller mistake. Moving the check into the constructor (or __post_init__) closes it while keeping python's public __init__.

findings.title: python and dart share mutable, process-wide Servers constants; go AllServers is a mutable slice
findings.description: go's own docs explain the goal: the generated Server* values are shared package-level values, so immutability stops one caller corrupting the configuration for the whole process. java (Map.of/List.copyOf), kotlin (toMap), csharp (ReadOnlyDictionary + collection-expression IReadOnlyList), node (Object.freeze), ruby (frozen), php (fresh instance per call), rust/elixir (fresh values) and swift (value types) all meet it. python's ServerConfiguration/ServerVariable are frozen dataclasses but their `variables: Dict` and `enum_values: List` are plain mutable containers, and SERVER_0/SERVER_1/ALL are module-level, so `SERVER_1.variables['version'].enum_values.append('evil')` changes validation for every caller. dart's top-level `final server1 = ServerConfiguration(variables: {...})` uses non-const map/list literals and the constructor does not copy them, so `server1.variables[...]` and `enumValues.add(...)` mutate the shared value; `allServers` is a growable list. go's AllServers is an exported []*ServerConfiguration whose elements can be reassigned.

evidence.quote: a mutable variable would let one caller corrupt the configuration for the whole process

findings.title: ruby and elixir per-operation server variants accept any value or nil for an enum variable and emit a malformed host
findings.description: In java/kotlin/csharp/php/dart/rust/swift/python/node the per-operation variant takes the generated enum type, so an out-of-enum value cannot be constructed (python fails with AttributeError on .value). ruby's GetStagingPetInfoServerStagingServer.new(environment:, version:) stores any object and calls .to_s with no check against the module constants, so 'evil' or nil goes into the URL (nil gives `https://.example.com/api/`). elixir's `defstruct [:environment, :version]` has no @enforce_keys and url/1 calls to_string/1 without a guard, so `%StagingServer{}` resolves to `https://.example.com/api/` and any string is accepted. go has the same empty-struct result through zero values, but that is a language default (forced). The global ServerConfiguration validates enums in all 12; the per-operation path validates nothing in these dynamic languages.

findings.note: done in elixir, ruby; still open for go

findings.title: AGENTS' reason that swift's date-time decoding 'cannot be made strict' is false: swift maps `format: date` to String, not Foundation.Date
findings.description: AGENTS.md:365-370 closes date-time input strictness by saying swift 'maps both `format: date` and `format: date-time` to one `Foundation.Date`, so it needs the date-only parse fallback'. In fact BetterSwiftCodegen.java:74 maps `date` to `String`, and only `DateTime` maps to `Date`. The `.custom` dateDecodingStrategy, including the `yyyy-MM-dd` fallback in ObjectSerializer.swift:69-79, therefore only ever runs for date-time fields. Swift accepts `"2024-01-01"` as a date-time (midnight UTC) for no reason any language forces, unlike the stricter SDKs. The date-only fallback could be removed.

findings.title: Integer-enum members ignore the language's enum casing in csharp, node, go, rust and swift
findings.description: String-enum members follow each language's convention (csharp/node/rust `OnHold`, go `AvailabilityOnHold`, swift `onHold`). Integer-enum members come out as the raw `NUMBER_1`: csharp Priority.cs:20, node priority.ts, go `PriorityNUMBER_1` (priority.go:22), rust `NUMBER_1` (which needs Cargo.toml `non_camel_case_types = "allow"`), swift `case NUMBER_1` instead of `number1`. dart (`number1`) and elixir (`:number_1`) apply their convention to int enums too. java/kotlin/php/python/ruby use UPPER_SNAKE for all enums and are consistent.

findings.title: Over-broad reserved-word mangling renames legal identifiers: swift `_type`, dart `type_`, php `$and_/$or_/$class_/$return_`, ruby `_and/_or/_not`
findings.description: loadReservedWords lowercases every entry (AbstractBetterCodegen.java:1446-1460). swift.txt lists `Type`, `Self`, `Any` and `Protocol`, so the plain field name `type` is escaped: ApiResponse is `_type` (ApiResponse.swift:13), although `var type` is legal Swift (only `.Type` is special). dart.txt lists `type` and `Function`, giving `type_` (api_response.dart:12), although neither is a reserved word in Dart. php escapes `and/or/class/return` to `$and_`, `$or_`, `$class_`, `$return_` (EdgeCases.php:36-48), although a `$`-sigiled property and PHP 8 named arguments both allow keywords. ruby escapes `and/or/not` to `_and`, `_or`, `_not` (edge_cases.rb:79-81), although `obj.and` is valid Ruby. Only `class` is a real clash, with Object#class. Meanwhile java, kotlin, csharp, go, node, python (where it is a real keyword) and elixir keep `type` and `and`. The extra renames change the public field name with no language feature forcing them. The prefix-versus-suffix escape style also differs among languages that do escape.

findings.title: `format: int32` range is enforced by 5 SDKs; swift (Int), python, dart, php, ruby, elixir and node accept and re-send values outside int32
findings.description: Order.quantity, Defaults.retries and similar int32 fields reject `3000000000` in java (verified, JsonMappingException), kotlin (toIntOrNull gives null, then throws), csharp (int), go (int32) and rust (i32). swift maps `integer` to `Int`, which is 64-bit (BetterSwiftCodegen.java:66-67), even though it maps int64 to `Int64` and Swift has Int32. python StrictInt is unbounded and could use conint. dart/php/ruby/elixir/node have only a 64-bit or arbitrary integer and never range-check. The same out-of-range wire value is rejected by 5 SDKs and accepted, then echoed back, by 7. swift's choice is clearly unforced.
findings.suspected_forced_reason: dart/php/ruby/elixir/node lack a native int32 type (could still range-check); swift and python are unforced

findings.title: elixir emits no field-level description or example, contrary to AGENTS 'Model field docs carry the scalar example in all 12'
findings.description: AGENTS.md:280 says field examples are present 'in all 12'. elixir/models/order.ex has zero `example` occurrences, and none of Order's 4 examples (10, 198772, 7, approved) appears. Field descriptions (Pet.homepageUrl, EdgeCases.permissionsNote, retryAfter) are missing too. Category's x-examples appear as module-level `## Small breed` sections with no mention of the `name` field. T3-5 ('elixir struct fields have no per-field doc slot') is undercut by R6-3, which already renders per-field `**Deprecated field**` notes inside @moduledoc. The same moduledoc list could carry each field's description and example.

findings.title: elixir's model-level `@deprecated` attaches to the next function (defstruct's __struct__), not to the module
findings.description: elixir/models/model.mustache:332-334 (and :490-492) emit `@deprecated "This schema is deprecated."` just before `@type t` and `defstruct`. In Elixir, @deprecated is a function attribute: it applies to the next `def`, and defstruct expands to `def __struct__/0,1`. The deprecation therefore lands on __struct__ (or the next generated function), which users never call directly; `%Tag{}` expands at compile time and gives no warning, and the module is not marked deprecated in docs. The idiomatic module-level marker is `@moduledoc deprecated: "…"` (doc metadata), which is close to the R6-3 moduledoc approach. The other 11 SDKs mark the type itself. This is plausible from reasoning; elixir is not available locally to verify.

findings.title: go deprecation markers on models, data methods and Options params are not a separate 'Deprecated:' paragraph, so go tooling does not see them
findings.description: go/models/model.mustache:80-82 (and the oneOf/anyOf variants at :428/:494) put `// Deprecated: This schema is deprecated.` directly under the description line with no blank `//` line between them. go/doc, staticcheck SA1019 and gopls recognize a deprecation only when a paragraph STARTS with 'Deprecated: '. That rule is staticcheck's split of the comment text on blank lines, recalled from its source and not run here because go is not installed on this machine. As emitted, tag.go:16-17 is one paragraph starting 'Tag Tags are…', so Tag is not flagged as deprecated. The same pattern appears on the FindPetsByStatus and GetPetById data methods (pet_api.go:677-678, 1149-1151) and the Options field (find_pets_by_status_options.go:7-8). The *WithHTTPInfo variants (pet_api.go:704-705) do include the blank `//` and are recognized. For the deprecated field Pet.Status, a blank NON-comment line between the `/* Status … */` block and `// Deprecated:` (pet.go:68-70) splits the comment groups, so the field's doc loses its description. AGENTS says go uses a '`// Deprecated:` doc paragraph'. That holds only for the WithHTTPInfo variants.

findings.title: kotlin and ruby strip null entries nested inside free-form model values; AGENTS' closed 'free-form null retention' item mislabels the split

findings.title: python raises a runtime DeprecationWarning whenever a deprecated field is set, including when the SDK decodes a server response

A validator runs on model_validate, so every Pet response that contains `status` emits a warning, even if the caller never touches the field. Under the common `-W error` or pytest `filterwarnings = error`, deserializing a normal server response raises. The other 11 SDKs warn only at compile or doc time when user code references the member. pydantic's own `Field(deprecated=...)` warns on attribute access, which is the closer equivalent.
