findings.title: ruby (Types::Any) and elixir models do no type or enum validation on construction, and go enums never validate on encode, so wrong-typed values reach the wire
findings.description: Every optional ruby attribute is `Types::Any.optional` (e.g. pet.rb:81, order.rb:68-77). Required ones are `Types::Required`, which only checks non-nil. Only INLINE enums use `Types::String.enum`, and $ref enums (favorite_color, availability) are Any. So `Pet.new(name: 123, photo_urls: [1])` or `Order.new(quantity: 'x')` builds and serializes `"name":123` with no error. OPENAPI_TYPES checking runs only on deserialize. elixir structs are untyped, and sanitize_for_serialization emits whatever is stored: an unknown inline-enum atom goes out as its name, and an unknown standalone-enum atom hits a FunctionClauseError in value/1. go enum types have UnmarshalJSON validation but no MarshalJSON, so `OrderStatusEnum("bogus")` is sent. python validates on construction and assignment (validate_assignment), node in the constructor, php through typed properties, and the static languages through their types.

findings.title: ruby request bodies send a DateTime in non-canonical form because `when Date` matches DateTime first

DateTime is a subclass of Date, so a DateTime value takes the Date branch and is sent as `object.to_s`, i.e. `2024-01-01T12:30:45+00:00` with no `.000`, instead of DEFAULT_DATETIME_FORMAT `%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S.%3N%:z`. Verified with ruby: `case DateTime.new(...) when Date` matches. The DateTime half of the second arm is dead code. Model attributes are `Types::Any`, so a DateTime assigned to a date-time field such as Order.ship_date reaches this path. The parameter path (stringify, :187) has no Date arm and is correct.

findings.title: swift: everything after `@available(*, deprecated)` is dropped from a deprecated data method's documentation (externalDocs, Parameters, examples), and blank lines split doc blocks
findings.description: The swift api template emits `@available(*, deprecated, …)` right after the summary/notes and BEFORE the externalDocs, `- Parameters:` and example lines. Verified by building a module with swiftc -emit-symbol-graph from the golden getPetById block: the docComment is only ["Find pet by ID", "Returns a single pet"]. The `- petId:` parameter doc and both examples are gone, and findPetsByStatus loses its externalDocs link and parameter list. Separately, the `{{#allParams}}{{#vendorExtensions.pluralExamples}}` line emits blank lines between example blocks, and Swift keeps only the LAST contiguous `///` block. Today this only bites the two deprecated ops, but any non-deprecated op with param examples would lose its summary. Other languages put the deprecation marker after the full doc (java/kotlin/csharp/dart) or in the doc itself. Fix: emit `@available` after the last `///` line (as the WithHTTPInfo variant already does) and make the example loop line standalone.

findings.title: Form-urlencoded and multipart field order on the wire differs (hash order, sorted, or random per process)
findings.description: setPetPreferences fields are nickname, tags, note, renewalDate in spec order. kotlin, csharp, python, ruby, node, php, dart and rust emit them in spec/insertion order. java builds the body in a HashMap, so the order is note, nickname, renewalDate, tags (verified on the JDK). go's url.Values.Encode and elixir's small-map Enum both sort keys: nickname, note, renewalDate, tags. swift iterates a [String: Any], which is randomly seeded per process. For multipart (uploadPetDocument: file, documentType, notes): java sends file, notes, documentType; elixir sorts; go (`range formFields` over a map), rust (HashMap<String, MultipartValue>) and swift ([String: Any]) are non-deterministic per call or per process. The governing rule asks for the same bytes on the wire. Ordered multipart matters to streaming servers that expect metadata before the file. kotlin, csharp and rust tests assert the exact order; java, swift, php, node and dart only assert contains(). Fix: use LinkedHashMap, ordered pairs or an ordered dict, and assert the exact body in every language.

findings.title: Multipart JSON part headers differ: csharp and dart add `; charset=utf-8` and change header order; kotlin adds a per-part Content-Length
findings.description: For addPetPhotos, the `metadata` part (encoding contentType application/json) is sent by java, python, ruby, php, node, go, rust, swift, elixir and kotlin as `Content-Disposition: form-data; name="metadata"` followed by `Content-Type: application/json`. csharp builds it with `new StringContent(json, Encoding.UTF8, "application/json")`, which sets `Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8`. Because Content-Disposition is removed and re-added afterwards, the Content-Type header also comes first. csharp already avoids this default for scalar parts (a comment in DefaultApiClient explains it), but not for the JSON part. dart uses `http.MultipartFile.fromString(..., contentType: MediaType('application','json'))`, and package:http always adds a charset parameter there, so dart also sends `application/json; charset=utf-8`. package:http also writes content-type before content-disposition and gives non-ASCII text fields an extra `content-type: text/plain; charset=utf-8` and `content-transfer-encoding: binary`. kotlin: Ktor's formData adds a `Content-Length` header to each binary part (checked with ktor-client-core 3.5.0: `[Content-Disposition=[form-data; name="files", filename="files"], Content-Type=[image/png], Content-Length=[2]]`). No other SDK sends a per-part Content-Length. AGENTS closes only the multipart filename and MIME type and kotlin's test depth, not these header bytes.

findings.description: Kotlin, csharp, php, node, dart (query and form) and rust (query and form) send query parameters, form fields and multipart parts in declaration order. The other 7 do not, and four of them send different bytes on different calls. java uses `new HashMap<>()` for queryParams, formBody and multipart, so getPetTag sends `filter,sizes,colors,revision`, setPetPreferences sends `note,nickname,renewalDate,tags`, addPetPhotos sends `metadata` before `files`, and uploadPetDocument sends `file,notes,documentType` (Java HashMap order computed). go ranges over a `map[string]any`, so query and multipart order is randomized per call; its form body is sorted by url.Values.Encode. swift iterates `[String: Any?]` dictionaries, so query and form order is randomized per process (two runs gave different orders). ruby is re-sorted alphabetically by Faraday (previous finding). elixir iterates small maps in sorted key order (query, form and multipart). rust multipart uses `HashMap<String, MultipartValue>`, which is randomized. python sends every allowReserved parameter after all the others. dart's http.MultipartRequest writes every text field before every file or JSON part. Ordered containers exist in every one of these languages (LinkedHashMap, slices, Vec, KeyValuePairs, keyword lists), and rust already uses an ordered Vec for query and form, so no language feature forces the difference.

findings.title: ApiResult equality and header mutability differ across the 12
findings.description:
ApiResult is the public return type of every `*WithHttpInfo` call, and its equality and immutability differ by language.
- Value equality: java (record), kotlin (data class), python (frozen dataclass), elixir (struct), php (loose ==).
- Reference equality: csharp (plain primary-ctor class, not a record), ruby, dart.
- No equality at all: rust (no PartialEq derive), swift (no Equatable conformance), node (plain interface object), go (map field makes == invalid).
- Headers: java and csharp take a read-only defensive copy, ruby freezes, rust, swift, php and elixir are immutable. python keeps a mutable `Dict` inside a `frozen=True` dataclass, so `hash(result)` raises TypeError and `result.headers[...] = ...` mutates it; python's own Configuration uses MappingProxyType for the same purpose. dart stores the mutable `response.headers` map as-is. kotlin stores the caller's map without copying.
None of this is forced: csharp can use `record`, rust can `derive(PartialEq)` (bounded on T), swift can add a conditional `Equatable where T: Equatable`, dart can override ==, and python/dart can wrap the headers read-only.

findings.title: Model equality on format:number fields depends on scale in java, kotlin and node, but not in csharp, python or the 7 float SDKs
findings.description: All 12 give models value equality, but the same two values compare differently. java's generated equals uses `Objects.equals(this.weightKg, other.weightKg)` on a BigDecimal, and kotlin's data class uses BigDecimal.equals. Both depend on scale: `1.5` and `1.50` are unequal and hash differently, so Pets decoded from `{"weightKg":1.5}` and `{"weightKg":1.50}` (Jackson keeps the text's scale) are not equal. node's Decimal is a branded string compared by `===`, so a user-built `Decimal("1.50")` does not equal a decoded `1.5` (JSON.parse canonicalises it to "1.5"). csharp (`decimal` equality and hash), python (verified: `Decimal('1.5') == Decimal('1.50')` with equal hashes) and the seven native-float SDKs treat them as equal. Not forced: java and kotlin can compare with `compareTo == 0` and hash `stripTrailingZeros()`, and node can normalise the Decimal string.

findings.description:
In kotlin, csharp, php, python, ruby, dart and swift a per-scheme authenticator subclasses the generic one (`PetStoreBearerAuthenticator : BearerAuthenticator`). It is therefore an instance of BearerAuthenticator and inherits the redacted representation under its own runtime class name, for example `PetStoreBearerAuthenticator(host=..., token=***)`.
- java: BearerAuthenticator, BasicAuthenticator and ApiKeyAuthenticator are `final`, so the wrapper extends BaseAuthenticator and delegates to a private BearerAuthenticator. `instanceof BearerAuthenticator` is false, and toString falls back to `PetStoreBearerAuthenticator@1b6d3586`.
- rust: the wrapper is a tuple struct `pub struct PetStoreBearerAuthenticator(BearerAuthenticator)` with no Debug impl (and no derive). It cannot be `{:?}`-formatted, against Rust API guideline C-DEBUG and unlike every other rust authenticator, which has a hand-written redacting Debug.
- go and node: the base String() / inspect hard-code "BearerAuthenticator{...}" / "BearerAuthenticator(...)", so the wrapper prints the base class name instead of its own.
None of this is forced: java's generic authenticators need not be final, rust can delegate Debug to self.0, and go and node can use the runtime type name.

findings.title: Per-scheme authenticators cannot be imported from the node or dart package; only java and kotlin test them
findings.description: Every SDK generates per-scheme authenticator classes (PetStoreBearerAuthenticator, AdminBasicAuthenticator, ApiKeyHeaderAuthenticator, SessionCookieAuthenticator, MachineAuthClientCredentialsAuthenticator, and others). They are public and importable in java, kotlin, csharp, php, ruby, go, rust (`pub use` in auth/mod.rs), swift and elixir. node's package.json `exports` only has ".", and src/index.ts re-exports only the generic Basic, Bearer and ApiKey authenticators plus OAuth2*. All 11 node per-scheme classes, plus BaseAuthenticator, OAuth2TokenManager and the ApiHttpResponse type (which the exported ApiClient interface returns), are therefore unreachable to consumers. dart's barrel exports base_authenticator and oauth2_token_manager but no per-scheme file, so using one needs a `package:.../src/` import, which the dart analyzer flags. python's `auth/__init__.py` does not re-export them either (they can still be imported by full module path). Coverage differs too: only java and kotlin PetApiTest use PetStoreBearerAuthenticator and AdminBasicAuthenticator, and the other 10 have no test of any per-scheme wrapper. Either export them uniformly with a test in each SDK, or stop generating them where they are unreachable.

findings.title: dart names the result variant `WithHTTPInfo`, against Dart naming style and its own `ApiHttpResponse`
findings.description: The result-returning variant is `addPetWithHttpInfo` or `add_pet_with_http_info` in java, kotlin, php, node, python, ruby, rust and elixir, and `AddPetWithHttpInfoAsync` in csharp. go and swift use `WithHTTPInfo`, which is idiomatic there: Go initialisms and the Swift API guidelines' uniform acronym case. dart emits `addPetWithHTTPInfo` for every operation. Effective Dart says the opposite: "DO capitalize acronyms and abbreviations longer than two letters like words" (`HttpClient`, `HttpRequest`). The same dart golden already follows that rule for its own `ApiHttpResponse` class and uses dart:io's `HttpClient`. The spelling comes from the dart api template and is not forced by any language feature.

findings.title: dart's barrel exports the no-auth sentinel (`noAuth`, `NoAuthAuthenticator`) as public API; the other SDKs hide it
findings.description: The NO_AUTH sentinel is meant to be internal: operations declared `security: []` pass it to suppress the client authenticator. python's docstring says it "never leaves the generated client; callers never see it", and ruby, php and elixir say the same. It is hidden in kotlin (`internal object NoAuth`), csharp (`internal sealed class NoAuth`), java (`protected static` in BaseApi), go (unexported), rust (`pub(crate)`), swift (internal) and node (not re-exported from the package root), and elixir marks it `@doc false`. dart declares `class NoAuthAuthenticator` and `const Authenticator noAuth` in src/auth/authenticator.dart, and the package barrel exports that file without `hide`. Dart consumers therefore get `noAuth` as a documented public symbol they can pass as a per-call `auth` to strip credentials from any operation, which no other strongly-encapsulating SDK allows. The fix is `export 'src/auth/authenticator.dart' hide noAuth, NoAuthAuthenticator;` or a library-private name. (php's public `Auth\NoAuth` and python's and ruby's public names come from those languages' lack of package-private visibility, though `@internal`, a leading underscore and `private_constant` are available.)

findings.title: swift Client has `withAuthenticator` but no `withToken`; the other 11 have both
findings.description: Each of the other 11 facades has both named factories: `withToken(host, accessToken[, transportOptions])` and `withAuthenticator(authenticator[, transportOptions])`. They appear as `Client.withToken` in java, kotlin, php and node, `WithToken` in csharp, `with_token` in python, ruby, rust and elixir, `Client.withToken` as a factory constructor in dart, and `NewClientWithToken` in go. swift keeps the static `withAuthenticator` but replaces `withToken` with a `convenience init(host:accessToken:transportOptions:)`. That is idiomatic Swift on its own, but the facade is now internally inconsistent: one factory is static and the other is an initializer. Either add `static func withToken(...)` to match its sibling, or drop `withAuthenticator` and use initializers for both.

findings.title: Only php's Client facade accepts an injected transport (plus a php-only Psr18ApiClient); the other 11 hard-wire a private DefaultApiClient per Client
findings.description: php's Client::__construct, withToken and withAuthenticator take `?ApiClient $apiClient` and ship a Psr18ApiClient adapter, so a php caller can share one transport and connection pool across several Client instances or bring a framework-managed client. In the other 11 the facade always does `new DefaultApiClient(transportOptions)` internally (dart even through a private constructor). A caller cannot share a pool between Clients or plug in a custom ApiClient through the facade, even though every SDK defines a public ApiClient interface. Combined with the documented T2-11 (the facades are not closeable), every Client built in those 11 SDKs owns a pool the caller can neither reuse nor release. The PSR-18 adapter is idiomatic php, but a facade-level transport parameter is not php-specific.

findings.title: SDKs disagree on whether they close a caller-supplied upload stream or file handle
findings.description: python (_multipart_part closes any .read()-able value), ruby (multipart_part ensure value.close), php (fclose on resource parts) and csharp (StreamContent disposed with the HttpRequestMessage) close a stream the caller passed in. go never closes an *os.File or io.Reader part, and even Seek(0)s the file first, which changes what is read compared with the others, which read from the current position. java closes an InputStream multipart part (try (stream)) but leaves a raw-body InputStream open (stream.readAllBytes() with no close). The same upload therefore leaves the handle open or closed depending on the language, and reuses or rewinds it differently.

findings.title: Timeout budget across a redirect chain: whole chain in go/node/swift, per hop in the other 9
findings.description: The same `timeout` gives different total budgets once redirects are followed. go's http.Client.Timeout covers the whole Do() including redirects. node builds one AbortSignal.timeout and spreads it into every redirect fetch. swift's timeoutIntervalForResource covers the whole URLSessionTask including delegate-followed redirects. java (redirectBuilder.timeout per hop), kotlin (per request), csharp (HttpClient.Timeout per SendAsync), python (urllib3 Timeout per request), ruby, php (max_duration per request), rust (per send) and elixir (a new Task per recursive hop) re-arm the deadline on every hop. With timeout=5s and up to 20 redirects, a call fails at about 5s in go/node/swift but can run about 105s elsewhere.
findings.suspected_forced_reason: go's Client.Timeout and swift's resource timeout are whole-transfer by library design. Either side could be made to match: per-hop with a per-request ctx/timeout in go and node, or a total budget in the manual-loop languages.

findings.title: Unsynchronized mutable auth state in the implicit and authorization-code authenticators (java/go/swift/csharp); kotlin uses @Volatile and rust a Mutex
findings.description: OAuth2ImplicitAuthenticator.accessToken and OAuth2AuthorizationCodeAuthenticator.tokenExchanged are written by setAccessToken/exchangeCode (typically on a callback thread) and read by getAuthHeaders on request threads. kotlin marks both @Volatile and rust wraps both in Mutex. java uses plain fields, which gives no happens-before, so a request thread can keep seeing null or false. go uses plain fields, a data race that `go test -race` flags and a torn read of a string header. swift's classes declare @unchecked Sendable over plain `var accessToken: String` and `var tokenExchanged: Bool`, a data race on a refcounted String. csharp uses plain fields. dart, node, php, ruby, python and elixir are not exposed: single-threaded, GIL-protected or immutable.
